title: The Applied Power Playbook Library
subtitle: Twenty complete plans for the conversations that shape your work, your money and your relationships

intro.heading: How to use this library
intro.html:
The book teaches the skills. This library puts them to work on twenty situations that come up again and again, and follows each one past the first conversation: through the yes, the half yes, the no, and the week when someone quietly changes their mind.

Don’t read it in order. When a situation is in front of you, read that playbook once, then fill in the blank worksheet at the end. By the time it’s filled in, you’ll know what you want and what you’ll do if you don’t get it.

The playbooks sit in four sections:

Section 1: Work and pay. 1. Asking for a raise. 2. Someone took credit for your work. 3. Telling your manager you’re at capacity. 4. Going for a promotion after being passed over. 5. Leaving a job well.

Section 2: Clients and money. 6. Raising your rates. 7. A dispute with a contractor or service provider. 8. Saying no to lending money to family or a friend. 9. Asking for money you’re owed. 10. A family favor that later becomes a debt.

Section 3: Relationships and family. 11. A difficult parent. 12. Sharing care of an aging parent with siblings. 13. In-laws. 14. The recurring fight with a partner. 15. An ex who keeps reopening practical agreements.

Section 4: Endings and transitions. 16. The apology and repair. 17. Asking for space. 18. Ending a relationship. 19. Considering reconnection. 20. Stepping back from a group or a role you’ve outgrown.

Every playbook has the same parts, in the same order:

  • One person’s situation.
  • A short Power Map: who decides, what each person needs, and where authority, resources and alternatives sit.
  • Their preparation sheet, filled in. It includes The Clean Ask (say what you want, give the relevant reason, leave room for a real answer) and The No-Agreement Plan (what you will do if the answer is still no).
  • A realistic conversation, then four branches: they agree, partly agree, refuse, or agree and then backtrack.
  • A follow-up message built on The Smallest Agreed Step (a useful next action, with clear agreement on exactly what it covers).
  • What to do if agreement never comes, and a worksheet, filled in and then blank.

The people, businesses, pay figures and research results in the examples are fictional illustrations, not current market data. Use real sources for your own situation. Change the words until they sound like you.

Every move in this library passes The Four Fair Influence Tests: Is it honest? Do they know what they are agreeing to? Can they make a real choice without unfair pressure or punishment? Am I using my power responsibly? Nothing here asks you to bluff, hide terms or punish a no.

Filling in the worksheets. Print the pages you need and write on them. Or, to fill them in on screen, add your answers in a PDF app that supports text annotations. The pages have no fill-in boxes, so you can’t just click and type. Open the file in your PDF app and pick its text tool (often called Add Text, Text Box, or Fill and Sign). Click on a writing line, type your answer, then save a copy under a new name. Save it somewhere private, not on a shared device or account.

Two cautions. Keep any notes or saved messages somewhere private, and check who else can open your phone, computer or accounts. And for legal, financial or medical questions, these playbooks help you prepare; a qualified professional gives the advice.

Safety and support: If there is fear, threats, physical harm, stalking, or control of your money or devices, a better conversation is not the answer. Stop using scripts, read Chapter 11, When Pressure Becomes Danger, and get help suited to the situation. In the US, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788, from a device the other person can’t access. For suicide or self-harm concerns, call or text 988. In immediate danger, call 911. This box applies to every playbook in this library.

intro.heading: Your reusable preparation page
intro.html:
Use this with the completed preparation sheet in your chosen playbook, then use that playbook’s worksheet for the details.

Check first: Keep this somewhere private, away from shared devices or accounts. If someone checks your things, prepare in your head or with safe support.

What I’m assuming, or still need to ask: ______________________________

sections.title: Work and pay
sections.intro: These five playbooks cover the conversations that decide what your work earns you: money, credit, time and options.

playbooks.title: Asking for a raise

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Danielle is forty-one and coordinates shipping for a furniture distributor. When the import specialist, Phil, left in January, she took over the customs paperwork for every overseas container. Nobody replaced him. Nobody changed her pay. She earns $54,000.

She has meant to raise it since spring. Every month there’s a reason to wait: the busy season, a slow quarter, her manager’s vacation. The timing never feels right, so the conversation never happens.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Danielle knows her job has grown, and she knows roughly what the market pays. She knows her manager, Nadine, can recommend a raise, and that the owner, Stan, approves anything above the yearly cost-of-living increase.

She doesn’t know whether there’s money in this year’s budget, whether Nadine will back her, or what her coworkers earn.

Nadine needs imports to keep moving without a new hire, and she needs to look sensible to Stan. Stan needs to control costs without losing people who know the system. Danielle’s alternative is real but unbuilt: other companies are hiring, but she hasn’t applied anywhere. That means she can’t mention another offer, because she doesn’t have one.

The most useful thing on this map: Nadine can’t say yes on her own, and Stan will question any number she brings him. So every figure Danielle uses needs a source on paper.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Danielle’s sheet, filled in.

  • What I want: Pay that matches the job I’m doing now.
  • Market pay, and where each number came from: Government wage data for logistics coordinators in my area (in the US, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes pay by job and region): middle of the range about $59,000. Five current job listings with posted pay: $58,000 to $66,000, and the two that mention customs are at the top. A former coworker at another distributor shared his range when I asked.
  • My contribution evidence: Customs filing for all overseas containers since January, about forty so far, with no held shipments. Caught a duplicate freight charge in May; the carrier credited $3,100. Trained the new warehouse clerk on the shipping system.
  • My number: $62,000.
  • My floor (private): $58,500 now, with a written review in six months.
  • Who recommends, who approves, and when: Nadine recommends. Stan approves. Next year’s budget is set in October.
  • The Clean Ask: “Since January I’ve handled all the customs paperwork as well as my own job. Coordinators who do both are paid $58,000 to $66,000 in this area. I’m asking for $62,000.”
  • If base pay is stuck, what else is worth having: The title “Logistics and Customs Coordinator.” The company paying for a customs course. One remote day a week.
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “We might hire a customs person”: ask whether that’s planned this year, and point out the work is mine until then. “I need to check”: agree a date and put it in writing.
  • My No-Agreement Plan: If there’s no raise and no written path by the October budget, I’ll start applying for customs coordinator jobs in November.
  • The one thing I won’t do: Hint at an offer I don’t have.
  • Fairness check: Everything here is true. I’d be fine with Nadine reading this sheet.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Danielle sent a calendar invite titled “Pay conversation,” so Nadine would know the topic and not feel ambushed.

Danielle: “I’ve brought one page, so this won’t take long. It’s about my pay, now that customs is part of my job.”

Nadine: “I wondered if this was coming. Go ahead.”

Danielle: “Since Phil left in January, I’ve filed customs for about forty containers, with no held shipments. In May I caught a duplicate freight charge, and the carrier credited $3,100. Listings that include customs work pay $58,000 to $66,000 around here. I’d like my pay to move to $62,000.”

She stops there. Nadine reads the page. Danielle lets the quiet sit instead of filling it.

Nadine: “I’ll be honest. Stan has talked about hiring a customs specialist and taking it off your desk.”

Danielle: “I’d rather know that now. Is it likely to happen this year?”

Nadine: “Probably not. Nobody’s posted the job.”

Danielle: “Then for now the work is mine, and I’m asking to be paid for the job as it is. If a specialist is hired later, we can look at my role again then.”

Nadine: “That’s fair. But I don’t know where $62,000 sits in our pay bands. I need to check before I say anything to Stan.”

Danielle: “That makes sense. How long do you need?”

Nadine: “A couple of weeks. Payroll has the bands.”

Danielle: “Then here’s a suggestion. You check the bands, and we meet again on the 30th. I’ll email that today with the page attached, so you have it if Stan asks.”

Nadine: “The 30th, then. I can’t tell you what Stan will say.”

Danielle: “Understood. Either way, I’d like to hear it from you.”

Danielle has no raise yet. The hiring question is out in the open, her manager is checking the numbers, and there’s a meeting on the calendar.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Thank them, then get it in writing. “Thank you. Could you send me a short email with the new salary and the start date? And when would we next look at my pay?” Check your first new paycheck. If it’s wrong, raise it that week, not three months later.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html:
Say Nadine comes back with $58,000. Don’t accept on the spot, and don’t reject it either.

Try saying: “Thank you for moving on this. It’s still below the range for the job. Could we get to $60,000, or agree on $58,000 now with a written review in six months?”

If the base pay truly can’t move further, look at the whole package. A one-time bonus, a title change, paid training, a better schedule or extra time off often come from different budgets. Take them if they’re worth it to you, but say plainly that pay is still the question, and put the review date in writing.

If your pay is set by a union contract or a public pay scale, the rate for each step usually can’t be negotiated. Ask about what can move instead. Are you on the right step for your experience? Should your job be classified higher, given the work you now do? Does acting or lead pay apply? Your union representative or HR can check, and mistakes in step placement do happen.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
Most refusals come as one of a handful of lines. Here is a calm reply to each.

  • “It’s not in the budget.” “Understood. When is the budget set, and can my request be on the list when it is?”
  • “Now isn’t the right time.” “What would need to be true for us to move forward?”
  • “We have to be fair across the team.” “I agree. To me, fair means pay matches the work. If my work doesn’t stand out, I’ll let it go. If we’re all below market, maybe the whole team’s pay needs a look.”
  • “Your performance doesn’t justify it.” “What specifically would have made this a different conversation? I’d like to leave with a list.”
  • “That’s above market.” “Could you share the figures you’re using? Here are mine. I’m happy to compare.”
  • “You just had a raise.” “I appreciated it. It matched the job I had then. The job has grown since.”
  • “We’re in a hiring freeze.” “Does that cover pay for current staff, or only new hires?”
  • “Show me another offer.” “I’m not job hunting to prove a point. I’d rather stay, which is why I’m here. What else would you want to see from me?”
  • “That’s more than I make.” “Thank you for telling me. My number comes from the market and the work, not from anyone else’s pay.”

If the answer is still a flat no, ask for a review date before you leave. “I’d like to come back to this. Could we put a date on the calendar three months from now, and agree on what you’d want to see from me by then?”

One rule holds through all of it. Never invent an offer or bluff about leaving. If a bluff gets called, you’re left with less than you started with, and your manager’s trust goes with it.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
At the meeting on the 30th, Nadine offers $60,000 from the first of next month and confirms it by email that afternoon. Two paychecks later, nothing has changed. When Danielle asks, Nadine says Stan now wants to wait for the budget.

Point to the record once, then ask about what happens next. Don’t argue about who promised what.

Try saying: “On the 30th you emailed that my pay would move to $60,000 from the 1st. It hasn’t shown up. What changed, and what’s the new date?”

If Stan reversed it, ask to speak with him, and tell Nadine first so nobody feels gone around. “I’d like to talk to Stan about this directly. I wanted you to hear that from me before I ask him.”

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
The same day, a short note that names the step and the date:

“Hi Nadine, thanks for your time today. As we discussed, you’ll check where $62,000 sits in the pay bands, and we’ll meet again on the 30th. The one-page summary is attached in case Stan asks for it. Danielle”

If the meeting on the 30th gets canceled or never booked, follow up within a few days: “Hi Nadine, checking in on my pay request. We didn’t get to meet on the 30th, and I want to make sure it hasn’t slipped. When can we reschedule?”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html:
Danielle’s line is already written: if there’s no raise and no written path by October, she starts applying in November. She doesn’t announce it as a threat. She simply does it.

If she gets a real offer, she can decide whether to tell Nadine honestly (Playbook 5 covers that). If she comes to believe her pay is being held back because of her race, sex, age or another protected trait, or as payback for raising a concern, that is a different problem. She should talk to HR or an employment lawyer.

If the job won’t pay for the work, finding one that will isn’t a failure. Chapter 18, Build Alternatives Before You Need Them, shows how to build that option early.

parts.heading: Worksheet: Raise case one-pager
parts.html:
Completed example: Danielle

  • My job now, compared with when my pay was last set: Shipping plus all customs paperwork (customs added in January).
  • Market pay and sources: BLS data, middle about $59,000 / five listings, $58,000 to $66,000 / former coworker’s range.
  • Three contributions with dates: Jan onward, customs for about forty containers / May, $3,100 freight credit / March, trained new clerk.
  • My number: $62,000. My floor: $58,500 plus written six-month review.
  • Recommends: Nadine. Approves: Stan. Budget date: October.
  • Other things worth having: Title change, customs course, one remote day.
  • Answer date agreed: The 30th.
  • My No-Agreement Plan: No raise or written path by October, I apply elsewhere in November.

Blank copy

  • My job now, compared with when my pay was last set: ______________________________
  • Market pay and sources: ______________________________ ______________________________
  • Three contributions with dates: ______________________________ ______________________________ ______________________________
  • My number: ______________ My floor: ______________
  • Recommends: ______________ Approves: ______________ Budget date: ______________

Check first: Keep this sheet and your contribution record somewhere private that you control, not only on a work computer. Follow your employer’s rules about company files, and don’t forward confidential documents to a personal account.

playbooks.title: Someone took credit for your work

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Jun is thirty-four and does customer research for a regional grocery chain. Over six weeks he ran the surveys, read every comment, and built a deck showing that shoppers were quitting the loyalty app because of one confusing screen. He emailed it to his manager, Margot, on the 4th.

On the 12th, Margot presented it to the vice president, Audrey. Jun wasn’t invited. A colleague who was there told him afterward that Margot said “what I found” more than once and never mentioned his name. Audrey has since emailed Margot: “Great insight. Let’s do more of this.”

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Jun knows he built the deck. His email from the 4th and the file history show it. He checks them in approved work systems and keeps any private contribution notes in his own words, without copying confidential files. He doesn’t know exactly what Margot said. His account is secondhand, and the colleague may have missed something. Managers often present their team’s work, and that is normal. The problem is a pattern where the person deciding his future never learns who did the work.

Margot decides who presents to Audrey, and she writes Jun’s review. Audrey decides projects and promotions above that. Margot needs to look good to Audrey. That gives Jun something to offer: a manager whose team is known for strong work looks good too.

Jun’s alternatives are limited but real: he can make his work visible in the team’s normal channels, ask Audrey for a career conversation, or, over time, move teams. He wants accurate credit and a seat at the next presentation. He doesn’t need a confession.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Jun’s sheet, filled in.

  • What I want: My name on decks I build, and ten minutes to present the follow-up findings to Audrey in October.
  • The facts I can point to: Email to Margot on the 4th with the deck attached. File history with my name. Survey tool account in my name.
  • What I’m guessing: What Margot actually said. I’ll leave the colleague out of it.
  • The Clean Ask: “I’d like my name on decks I build, and I’d like to present the October findings to Audrey myself. Audrey decides future projects, so I’d like her to know who did the work.”
  • Who decides: Margot, on both. Audrey, on anything bigger.
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “It’s team work”: “You present for the team. This one was mine start to finish.” “Are you accusing me?”: “I’m asking for a fix going forward.”
  • My No-Agreement Plan: Post progress in the team’s weekly update so others see the work. Ask Audrey for a career conversation once, telling Margot first. If it’s still happening by spring, look at internal openings.
  • The one thing I won’t do: Call her a liar, or complain about her to coworkers.
  • Fairness check: I’m asking openly for something I could explain to anyone.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Jun: “Do you have fifteen minutes? I’d like to talk about the loyalty deck.”

Margot: “Sure. Audrey loved it, by the way.”

Jun: “I’m glad it landed. I’d like to talk about how my work gets presented from here on.”

Margot: “What do you mean?”

Jun: “I ran the surveys and built the deck, and I sent it to you on the 4th. My understanding is my name didn’t come up with Audrey. I’m not asking about what was said. I’d like my name on decks I build, and to present the October findings myself.”

Margot: “Jun, I present for the team. That’s my job. Everything we do is team work.”

Jun: “I understand you present for the team. This one was mine from start to finish.”

Margot: “Are you saying I took credit for it?”

Jun doesn’t argue about her intent. He goes back to what he wants next.

Jun: “I’m saying Audrey doesn’t know who did the analysis, and that affects my review and my next project. I’d like to fix that going forward.”

Margot: “Her meetings are short. I can’t bring everyone in.”

Jun: “Ten minutes on the findings would be enough. You’d still lead the meeting.”

Margot: “I’ll think about it. I’m not promising the slot.”

Jun: “Fair. Could my name go on the cover page and in the notes from now on?”

Margot: “That’s fine.”

Jun: “Thanks. Could you let me know about October by Friday?”

Margot: “Friday.”

Margot is a little stiff for the rest of the day. Jun has his name on future work and a decision date.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Confirm it in writing, then prepare well. A clear, useful ten minutes in front of Audrey does more for your credit than any conversation about credit. Lead with the point and keep it short (Chapter 19, Be Credible, Visible, and Clear).

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Margot agrees to the name on the cover but not the meeting. Take what you got and widen it gently. Ask to be copied when your work goes upward: “When you send my decks on to Audrey, could you copy me, so I can answer questions?” Send a short monthly summary of your work to Margot that she can forward easily. You’re making it simple for your name to travel with the work.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
Margot says, “Names don’t go on decks here. It’s all team output.” Don’t escalate in the room.

Try saying: “I hear you. I’ll keep sharing progress in the team update so everyone can see where the project stands.”

Then make your work visible through ordinary channels: the weekly update, the project tracker, any meeting where you can speak to your own work. If that’s not enough, ask Audrey for a short career conversation, and tell Margot first: “I’d like to ask Audrey for twenty minutes about my development. I wanted you to know before I asked.” In that conversation, talk about your work and your goals, not about Margot.

If you believe credit is being withheld because of a protected trait, or as payback for raising a concern, talk to HR or an employment lawyer.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
Margot says yes to October. The week before, she says Audrey’s agenda is full and she’ll cover the findings herself.

Try saying: “We’d agreed I’d present the findings. If the slot’s gone, could I join for the five minutes on findings? Or I can send Audrey a one-page summary with you copied.”

If the story shifts (“I never said you’d present”), point to the email once and ask what happens now. Chapter 8, When the Story Keeps Changing, covers this.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html: “Hi Margot, thanks for talking today. To confirm: from now on my name goes on the cover and notes of decks I build, and you’ll let me know by Friday about my presenting the October findings to Audrey. Jun”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: One incident is a moment. Months of it is a pattern. Jun’s contribution log, kept every Friday, will show which it is. If his work keeps reaching Audrey without his name by spring, his No-Agreement Plan moves on: he looks at internal openings and builds relationships with people who see his work directly (Chapter 20, Build Allies Without Creating Debts). A job where the decision-makers know what you do is worth looking for.

parts.html:

playbooks.title: Telling your manager you're at capacity

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Reggie is fifty-three and the technology support lead for a small school district. He covers four schools. Over eighteen months, three jobs landed on him one at a time: setting up tablets for every third grader, running the new door-badge system, and covering the help desk on Thursdays after a coworker went part-time. Nothing came off his list.

He now works most evenings. Last month two repair tickets sat for a week, and a principal complained. Then the district office asked for the summer laptop replacement, all 600 machines, and his manager, Phyllis, forwarded it with one line: “You’re the best person for this.”

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Reggie knows what was added and when. He knows the quality is slipping. He doesn’t know whether Phyllis has ever seen the whole list, whether there is money for summer help, or whether his coworker’s hours will come back.

Phyllis decides his priorities. The district office controls hiring and budget. Phyllis needs the laptops done and no more calls from principals. Those needs work in Reggie’s favor: a missed ticket makes Phyllis look bad too.

Reggie can’t refuse his job, and he doesn’t want to. What he can do is stop absorbing work in silence, and hand the choice about what matters most back to the person whose job it is to make it.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Reggie’s sheet, filled in.

  • What I want: A decision on what comes off, waits or gets help, before I start the laptop job.
  • The facts: Workload map (below). Three jobs added, none removed. Two tickets late last month.
  • The Clean Ask: “Three big jobs have been added since last spring and nothing came off. I can’t do the laptop replacement well on top of everything else. I’d like us to decide together what comes off or waits.”
  • Two options I can offer: A: I take the laptops if Thursday help desk moves to someone else until August. B: I keep everything, and the laptops start the week school ends, with a summer temp for setup.
  • Who decides: Phyllis on priorities. District office on a temp.
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “Everyone’s stretched”: “That’s why I want to be clear about what I can do well.” “It’s only temporary”: “Then let’s put an end date on it.” “You’re the best at this”: “Thank you. Even so, all of it at once is more than I can do well.”
  • My No-Agreement Plan: Work my contracted hours. Each Friday, send Phyllis a short list of what got done and what didn’t. If nothing changes by the end of the school year, ask about my title and pay, and look at other districts.
  • The one thing I won’t do: Say yes in the hallway and complain later.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Reggie: “Phyllis, before I start on the laptops, I want to look at my whole workload with you. Here’s everything on my plate.”

Phyllis: “Okay. That’s a long list.”

Reggie: “The tablets, the badge system and Thursday help desk were all added since last spring. Nothing came off. That’s why two tickets sat last month. I can’t add 600 laptops and do any of it well.”

Phyllis: “Everyone’s stretched, Reggie. The whole district is short.”

Reggie: “I know. That’s why I want to be clear about what I can actually deliver. Which of these matters most to you?”

Phyllis: “All of it matters.”

Reggie: “Then let me give you two ways it could work. I take the laptops if someone else covers Thursdays until August. Or I keep everything and start the laptops the week school ends, with a summer temp for setup.”

Phyllis: “There’s no money for a temp. And Thursdays is only until Karen’s hours come back.”

Reggie: “When is that?”

Phyllis: “I don’t know. Maybe January.”

Reggie: “Then could Thursdays move to Luke from the high school until the laptops are done? I’ll train him for an hour.”

Phyllis: “Luke will complain.”

Reggie: “He might. Without some change, the laptops will be late, and the tickets will slip again.”

Phyllis: “Fine. Luke takes Thursdays through August. I’ll ask about a temp, but don’t count on it.”

Reggie: “Thanks. I’ll send you a note with that, and the laptop timeline.”

Reggie didn’t get the temp. He got one task off his list, with an end date, and a manager who has seen the whole picture.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Confirm it in writing that day, and put a date in your calendar to check how it’s going. If the old task drifts back (“Luke’s out, can you grab Thursday?”), raise it the first time, not the fifth.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Phyllis moves Thursdays to Luke but asks Reggie to “just take the help desk calls Luke can’t handle.” That’s a small leak in the agreement. Name it kindly: “Happy to help with anything that’s truly stuck. Everyday Thursday calls should stay with Luke, or the help desk will land back on me.”

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
Phyllis says: “I need you to do all of it. Figure it out.”

Try saying: “I’ll do my best with the hours I have. Since I can’t do all of it at once, could you tell me which comes first? Otherwise I’ll go by what’s due soonest and send you a list each Friday.”

You’ve stated a plan, not a threat. Then follow it. The Friday list does two jobs: it shows Phyllis the trade-offs she’s choosing, and it gives you a record if questions come up later.

If you’re pushing past exhaustion and it’s affecting your health, talk to a doctor, and look at what support your employer offers.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
Two weeks later, Phyllis says Luke can’t do Thursdays after all. She doesn’t offer anything in its place.

Try saying: “We agreed Luke would cover Thursdays through August so I could do the laptops. If that’s off, the laptop timeline moves back two weeks. Which would you prefer?”

Don’t quietly absorb the change. An agreement that can be undone silently isn’t much of an agreement.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html: “Hi Phyllis, thanks for going through my workload. We agreed Luke will cover Thursday help desk through August and you’ll ask about a summer temp. Could the handover start next week, with training on Monday? I’ll send a proposed laptop timeline on Friday. Reggie”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: If every conversation ends with “do it all,” the answer is telling you something about the job. Reggie works his hours, sends his Friday list, and keeps a copy for himself. At the end of the school year he asks a different question: “My role has grown by three jobs. If it stays this size, I’d like to talk about my title and pay.” If that’s refused too, his No-Agreement Plan moves to other districts. Chapter 28, When They Still Say No, walks through the choices.

playbooks.title: Going for a promotion after being passed over

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Priscilla is forty-six and a senior claims adjuster at an insurance company. In the spring she applied to lead her team of eight. The job went to an outside hire. Her manager, Gordon, told her she was “not quite ready” and needed “more leadership exposure.”

For two years Priscilla has trained every new adjuster on the team, without the title. A second team lead role is expected to open next year when another lead retires.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Priscilla knows she was passed over and was given a vague reason. She doesn’t know what “ready” means to the people deciding, who exactly made the call, or whether the retirement will happen on time.

Gordon recommends. The regional director, Yvette, approves. HR sets the pay band for each level. Gordon needs strong leads who won’t need rescuing. Yvette needs someone she has seen handle hard cases or people problems.

This is the key point on Priscilla’s map: Yvette barely knows her. The outside hire may have had nothing over Priscilla except that the deciders had seen their work. Priscilla’s task for the next year is to turn “ready” into a short written list, then make sure the people deciding see her meet it.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Priscilla’s sheet, filled in.

  • What I want: To be the leading candidate for the next lead role, with clear criteria in writing.
  • What I’m not asking for: A reversal of the spring decision.
  • The Clean Ask: “I’d like to be ready for the next lead opening. Could we agree on what I’d need to show, specifically, and review it in six months?”
  • Questions to ask: What did “leadership exposure” mean in practice? Who made the final decision, and what did they see? Can I take on an acting or lead role in the meantime?
  • Evidence I already have: Trained six new adjusters in two years. Handled the flood claims backlog last fall.
  • Who decides: Gordon recommends, Yvette approves, HR sets the band.
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “We’ll see when it opens”: “I’d like to know the criteria now, so I can work toward them.”
  • My No-Agreement Plan: If there are no written criteria by year end, or I meet them and am passed over again with no clear reason, I’ll apply for lead roles at other insurers.
  • The one thing I won’t do: Criticize the person who got the job.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Priscilla: “Thanks for meeting. I’m not here to revisit the spring decision. I’d like to plan for the next lead opening.”

Gordon: “Good. I’m glad you’re still interested.”

Priscilla: “You said I needed more leadership exposure. What would that look like, specifically?”

Gordon: “Honestly, it’s partly presence. Yvette wants leads who can handle her meetings.”

Priscilla: “That helps. What would show that? Presenting at her monthly review, for example?”

Gordon: “That would be a start. Running a project with another team. And handling a formal complaint start to finish.”

Priscilla: “So three things: present at Yvette’s review, lead a cross-team project, and handle a formal complaint. If I do those by March, can we agree I’m the lead candidate for the next opening?”

Gordon: “I can’t promise the job. Yvette decides.”

Priscilla: “I understand. Could you agree that if I meet those three, you’ll recommend me?”

Gordon: “If you do all three well, yes. I’d recommend you.”

Priscilla: “Thank you. One more thing. I’ve trained six adjusters. Could that be made official, as a senior or training lead title?”

Gordon: “Maybe. That’s HR. Let me ask.”

Priscilla: “I’ll send you a note with the three items so we’re both working from the same list.”

She leaves without the job. She leaves with three concrete targets, a manager’s conditional recommendation, and a chance to appear in front of Yvette.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Confirm the list in writing, then get started fast, especially on anything that puts your work in front of the person who approves. Update your manager briefly as you finish each item, so the record builds as you go.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html:
Gordon gives the list but won’t commit to recommending her. Take the list anyway and ask for a review date. “Could we look at progress in March?” A list with a date still beats a feeling.

If the offer is a new title without new pay, a promotion in name only, say thank you and raise the gap right away. “Thank you. The new role brings more responsibility at the same pay. When will the pay catch up?” Ask when, not whether, and get the answer in writing. If pay is set by bands, ask which band the new title sits in and when you’ll move.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
Gordon won’t name criteria. “It’s a judgment call. You’ll know when you’re ready.”

Try saying: “I understand there’s judgment involved. Could you give me two or three examples of what a ready candidate does that I don’t yet?”

If he still can’t name anything, that tells you something. Ask HR how lead roles are filled, and whether there are written criteria for the level. Ask Yvette for a short career conversation, telling Gordon first.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
By March, Priscilla has done all three. Now Gordon says leads also need the company’s leadership certificate. This is the moving target you met in Chapter 10, Charm, Urgency, and the Slow Squeeze.

Try saying: “In September we agreed on three things, and I’ve done all of them. Is the certificate new for everyone, or just for this role? If it’s required, can we agree it’s the last item, with a date?”

Point to the written list once. Then ask for a decision on the terms you agreed.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html: “Hi Gordon, thanks for today. To confirm the three things you’d want to see before the next lead opening: present at Yvette’s monthly review, lead a project with another team, and handle a formal complaint start to finish. We’ll review progress in March, and you’ll ask HR about a training lead title. Priscilla”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: If Priscilla meets the criteria and the next role still goes elsewhere with no clear reason, her No-Agreement Plan applies. She now has three strong examples to bring to other employers. If she believes she’s being passed over because of age, sex, race or another protected trait, she should talk to HR or an employment lawyer.

playbooks.title: Leaving a job well

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Kurt is fifty-nine and has run purchasing at a parts manufacturer for fourteen years. A hospital system’s supply department has made him a written offer. He has asked for raises twice in three years and been told “next year” both times.

He has two decisions in front of him. First, whether to take the offer. Second, if he does, how to leave without burning fourteen years of relationships.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Kurt decides whether he goes. His manager, Arlene, decides how his notice is handled, and whether to make a counteroffer. The company’s policies decide things like when final pay arrives and whether unused vacation is paid out.

He knows the offer details because they’re in writing. He doesn’t know how Arlene will react, whether the company will ask him to leave the same day, or exactly what his employment agreement says about notice or working for others afterward.

Check first: Before you resign, read your employment agreement and handbook for notice periods, vacation payout and any restrictions on future work. If something is unclear, talk to an employment lawyer. Accept the new offer in writing, and confirm the start date and any background checks, before you tell your current employer.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Kurt’s sheet, filled in.

  • Is the offer real? Yes. Written, signed, start date confirmed.
  • Would a matching offer keep me? Honestly, no. Pay is only part of it. I’m not asking for a counteroffer.
  • What I want from the conversation: A clean exit, a good reference, and a handover I can be proud of.
  • The Clean Ask: “I’ve decided to resign. My last day will be the 28th. I’d like to use the next three weeks to hand everything over properly.”
  • Handover plan: A list of open orders and supplier contracts, who could take each one, and three training sessions for Alma, who covers when I’m away.
  • What I’ll offer beyond my last day: Phone questions for two weeks. Nothing more without pay.
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “What would it take to keep you?”: “I appreciate it. I’m not looking for a counteroffer.” “Can you stay two more months?”: “I can’t move my last day. I can make the handover thorough.”
  • Where I’m going: I’ll share it once I start. Not before.
  • My No-Agreement Plan: If they ask me to leave the same day, I’ll have my personal things ready and the handover list written, and I’ll offer it by email.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Kurt: “Arlene, I wanted you to hear this from me first. I’ve decided to resign. My last day will be the 28th.”

Arlene: “Oh. Wow. I didn’t see that coming.”

Kurt: “I know it’s a surprise. I want to thank you for putting me on the supplier review in 2019. I learned more from that than anything else here.”

Arlene: “Is it money? Because I can talk to Malcolm.”

Kurt: “I appreciate that. I’ve thought it through carefully, and I’m not looking for a counteroffer.”

Arlene: “Fourteen years, Kurt. After everything we’ve built, you’re leaving us with the spring contracts open?”

This is the ledger from Chapter 7: past support turned into a debt. Kurt agrees with the gratitude and keeps the decision.

Kurt: “I’m grateful for those fourteen years. That’s why I’m giving three weeks and a full handover. I’ve already listed every open contract and who could take it.”

Arlene: “Could you at least stay until the contracts are signed? That’s two months.”

Kurt: “I can’t move my last day. I can train Alma on all three spring contracts before I go, and take her calls for two weeks after.”

Arlene: “That’ll be tight.”

Kurt: “It will. I’ll send you the handover plan today, along with my resignation in writing.”

Arlene is disappointed and doesn’t hide it. Kurt didn’t over-explain, didn’t apologize for leaving, and didn’t let gratitude turn into staying.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Arlene accepts the date and the plan. Put both in writing that day, and follow through on every item. The last three weeks are what people remember.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Arlene accepts the date but keeps adding to the list: two new supplier negotiations “while you’re still here.” Name it. “I’d rather not start anything I can’t finish. Shall I set these up for Alma instead?”

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
Some companies ask a departing employee to leave the same day. That isn’t personal, and it’s why Kurt prepared. He stays polite, takes only his personal things, and sends the handover list by email. He doesn’t copy company files on his way out.

If, instead, they make a counteroffer, the honest answer depends on what you said. If you’ve decided, repeat it kindly. If you’d truly stay for the right terms, you could have said so before accepting the other job. Changing your mind afterward costs you trust in two places.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
Arlene agreed to three weeks and a handover. In week two she asks Kurt to train two more people “next month, on your own time, as a favor.” He’s already gone by then.

Try saying: “I’m glad to answer Alma’s questions for two weeks, as we agreed. Training beyond that I’d do as paid consulting. I can send you a rate if that helps.”

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
“Hi Arlene, as discussed, I’m resigning from my role as purchasing manager. My last day will be the 28th. Attached is my handover plan: open contracts, suggested owners, and three training sessions with Alma. After I leave, I’m happy to take Alma’s questions by phone for two weeks. Thank you for fourteen good years. Kurt”

Keep a private copy of your resignation. Keep company handover files in approved work systems, and follow your employer’s rules about copies.

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: On an exit, you don’t need their agreement. Leaving is your decision. What you can’t control is how they take it. If they’re cold for your last three weeks, do the handover anyway. That record belongs to you, and people remember it long after the awkwardness fades.

sections.title: Clients and money
sections.intro: These five playbooks cover money conversations with clients, contractors, friends and family, where the relationship and the money both matter.

playbooks.title: Raising your rates

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Sylvia is fifty and works as a freelance bookkeeper for fourteen small businesses. She charges $45 an hour and hasn’t changed it in three years. Her software costs have gone up twice. She has two referrals waiting because she has no time to take them on.

Her largest client is a family restaurant owned by Benny. It brings in about a quarter of her income. Benny is the one she’s most afraid to tell.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Sylvia decides her own price. Each client decides whether to stay. She knows her costs, her current rate, and that she’s turning work away. She doesn’t know who will leave.

Her alternatives are stronger than they feel. Two waiting referrals can be quoted at the new rate. She worked out that she could lose up to three small clients and still come out ahead. Benny is the real risk. Losing him would hurt, so she plans for that conversation separately.

Benny needs his books done right and on time, at a cost he can plan for. Sylvia can offer something he values: a fixed monthly fee he can budget, if he sends her receipts on time.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Sylvia’s sheet, filled in.

  • What I want: $58 an hour for new clients now, and for existing clients from March 1.
  • The reason I’ll give: Software costs, three years at the same rate, and the work has grown.
  • Notice: Letters go out in December. I picked that so clients can plan for the new year.
  • Order: New clients first, then small regulars, then Benny with a phone call after his letter.
  • The Clean Ask (as a statement): “Starting March 1, my rate will be $58 an hour. I’m telling you now so you have time to plan.”
  • What I can trade (not discount): A fixed monthly fee if receipts arrive weekly through the app. Weekly receipts save me time, so the fee can sit a little below what the new hourly rate would come to.
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “That’s a big jump”: “It is. I held it for three years.” “Others charge less”: “Some do. I can’t speak to their work.”
  • My No-Agreement Plan: If Benny leaves, I take both referrals and offer him a clean handover. If more than three clients leave, I review in June.
  • The one thing I won’t do: Offer a discount before anyone asks.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Benny called the day after his letter arrived.

Benny: “Sylvia, I got your letter. Fifty-eight an hour? Margins are tight in restaurants right now.”

Sylvia: “I know they are. I held my rate for three years while my costs went up. This brings it in line.”

Benny: “My brother-in-law’s bookkeeper charges forty.”

Sylvia: “She might. I can’t speak to her work. I’ve closed your books on time every month, and I caught the sales tax error last spring.”

Benny: “I’m not saying you’re not good. I just can’t plan for a bill that jumps around.”

Sylvia: “That I can help with. If you send receipts through the app every week instead of a box every quarter, I could do your books for a fixed $1,150 a month. You’d know exactly what it costs.”

Benny: “What do I pay now, roughly?”

Sylvia: “About $1,000 a month, but it changes. Quarter-end months run higher.”

Benny: “So a hundred and fifty more, but steady.”

Sylvia: “Yes. And less time for both of us at quarter end.”

Benny: “Let me talk to my wife. She does the receipts.”

Sylvia: “Of course. Could you let me know by the 15th? That gives me time to set it up for March.”

Benny didn’t say yes. Sylvia gave a real reason, offered a trade instead of a discount, and set a true deadline.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Send the new terms in writing, and update your invoices so the new rate is clear. For a fixed fee, write down what it covers and what costs extra.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Benny says yes to the fixed fee but asks to start in June. Decide whether that’s worth it to you. If you agree, put the date in writing. If you’d rather not, offer something smaller: “I can do March at the fixed fee. If the receipts aren’t weekly by June, we’ll go back to hourly.”

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
Benny says he’s moving to his brother-in-law’s bookkeeper.

Try saying: “I understand. Thank you for four good years. I’ll have everything ready to hand over by the end of February, so nothing gets missed.”

A clean handover protects your reputation and leaves the door open. Clients who leave over price sometimes come back.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
Benny agreed to the fixed fee from March. In April he pays $1,000 and writes “same as before” in the memo.

Try saying: “Thanks for the payment, Benny. It came in at $1,000, and our March agreement was $1,150 a month. Could you send the $150 difference with May’s?”

Keep it about the invoice, not about his character. If it happens again, talk before doing more work.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html: “Hi Benny, thanks for the call. My proposed fixed fee from March 1 is $1,150 a month for monthly bookkeeping and quarterly sales tax, with receipts through the app each week. Year-end and payroll filings would stay separate at $58 an hour. These terms aren’t agreed yet. Could you let me know by the 15th whether they work for you? Sylvia”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Some clients won’t agree to any increase. You’re allowed to let them go. Sylvia’s plan already counts on losing a few. Each one frees time for a referral at the new rate. Chapter 24, Clients, Customers, and Money Decisions, covers the habits that make the next increase easier.

playbooks.title: A dispute with a contractor or service provider

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Arturo is thirty-eight. He hired a contractor, Conrad, to redo his bathroom for a written quote of $14,500. Midway through, Conrad found rot under the floor and texted, “Subfloor’s bad, have to replace it, ok?” Arturo replied, “Ok, do what you need to.” No price was mentioned.

The final invoice is $19,800. Arturo has paid $11,500. Conrad wants the remaining $8,300 before he fixes grout that has already cracked near the tub.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Arturo knows the quote, has the texts and has photos of the rot and the cracked grout. He doesn’t know what a subfloor repair of this size should cost, what his contract says about changes, or what rules his state has about unpaid contractor bills.

Some of the extra is probably fair. The rot was real, and Arturo said yes to fixing it. Some may not be: the invoice also lists $1,900 for “upgraded fixtures” Arturo never chose.

Neither side decides alone. Conrad needs to be paid and wants a good reputation. Arturo needs the work finished properly and a bill he can understand. If they can’t agree, an outside process decides, which is slower and costs both of them.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Arturo’s sheet, filled in.

  • What I want: To pay fairly for the agreed work and the subfloor, not for fixtures I didn’t choose, and to have the grout fixed.
  • Line by line: Original quote, $14,500, agreed. Subfloor, $3,400 billed, agreed in principle, price never discussed. Fixtures upgrade, $1,900, never discussed.
  • Before deciding what to pay or hold back: I’ll ask a lawyer or my state’s consumer protection office how my contract and local rules affect my options.
  • My proposed payment: The remaining $3,000 on the original quote, with the disputed charges and the repair discussed separately, if that fits the advice I get.
  • The Clean Ask: “I want to pay you properly. I’ll pay the $3,000 left on the quote now. For the subfloor, I’d like a breakdown of hours and materials. I didn’t choose the fixture upgrade, so I’m not comfortable paying for it. And I’d like the grout fixed before final payment.”
  • Two options I’d accept: Subfloor at the breakdown cost and fixtures removed from the bill. Or keep the upgraded fixtures at the price of the originals.
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “Pay in full or I don’t come back”: “I’ll pay the undisputed part today. Send the breakdown, and I’ll answer by Thursday.”
  • My No-Agreement Plan: Call my state’s consumer protection office and check Conrad’s license with the state licensing board. Ask about mediation. For a large unresolved amount, talk to a lawyer before deciding anything.
  • The one thing I won’t do: Threaten a bad review to get a discount. An honest review afterward is fine. Using it as a threat is pressure.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Arturo: “Thanks for coming by. I went through the invoice and want to settle it fairly. Can we go through it line by line?”

Conrad: “It’s all there. The subfloor was a big job.”

Arturo: “I know, and I agreed you should fix it. We never talked about a price. Could you send me the hours and materials for that part?”

Conrad: “That’s just what it costs.”

Arturo: “I believe it was real work. I’d still like to see the breakdown before I pay $3,400.”

Conrad: “Fine. What about the rest?”

Arturo: “The fixture upgrade. I didn’t choose that, so I’m not comfortable paying for it. I can return them, or keep them at the price of the originals.”

Conrad: “The originals were out of stock. I made a call.”

Arturo: “I understand. I’d have liked to be asked. Today, I’ll pay the $3,000 left on the quote. Could you fix the grout this week?”

Conrad: “I’m not coming back until I’m paid in full.”

Arturo: “I’ll pay the undisputed part now and the rest as soon as we agree on it. Send me the breakdown, and I’ll answer by Thursday.”

Conrad: “I’ll send it. But the grout waits.”

Nothing is settled except the $3,000 and a breakdown on its way. Arturo didn’t pay the disputed amount to end the discomfort, and he didn’t refuse to pay what he owes.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Get the final amount in writing, then pay exactly that. Ask for a receipt marked “paid in full,” and keep it with the contract somewhere private, away from shared accounts or devices.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Conrad drops the fixtures to the original price but holds the subfloor at $3,400 with a thin breakdown. Decide whether the gap is worth fighting over. You might ask a second contractor what a fair price for that work would be. Then make one counteroffer in writing and let it stand.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: Conrad demands full payment and stops answering. Before deciding what to pay or hold back, talk to a lawyer or your state’s consumer protection office about the contract and local rules; contractors can sometimes take legal steps over unpaid bills. Keep the messages somewhere private. Put your questions and proposed resolution in one short letter or email. If the contractor threatens you or you feel unsafe, stop the exchange and see Chapter 11. In immediate danger, call 911.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
Conrad agrees to $17,900 and to fix the grout. Then a “final” invoice arrives at $18,600 with a new line for “disposal.”

Try saying: “On the 9th we agreed on a final total that included the grout repair. This invoice adds $700 for disposal, which we didn’t discuss. The agreed total is $17,900. I’ve paid $14,500, leaving $3,400, payable when the grout is done.”

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html: “Hi Conrad, thanks for going through the invoice. To confirm: I paid $3,000 today, which completes the original quote. You’ll send a breakdown of the subfloor hours and materials. My proposal is to return the upgraded fixtures or keep them at the original fixture price. You haven’t agreed to that yet. I’ll respond to the breakdown by Thursday. I’d like the grout near the tub fixed before final payment. Arturo”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Your options outside the conversation include your state’s consumer protection office, a complaint to the licensing board, mediation and small claims court for smaller amounts. Rules and limits vary, so check your local court’s website or ask a lawyer. Sometimes the fairest end is to pay a compromise, get the work finished by someone else, and stop spending evenings on it. That’s a choice, not a defeat.

playbooks.title: Saying no to lending money to family or a friend

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Noreen is sixty-two and a retired school librarian. Her friend of thirty years, Marla, calls to ask for $4,000. Marla’s hours were cut, and she’s behind on rent. Two years ago Noreen lent her $1,500. Marla paid back $600, and neither of them has mentioned the rest since.

Noreen lives on a pension. $4,000 is a large piece of her emergency savings.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Noreen alone decides what happens to her money. Marla decides how she responds to the answer. Noreen knows her own budget and the open $900. She doesn’t know Marla’s full situation, or whether other people are helping.

The honest test is simple: if this money never came back, would Noreen be fine, and would the friendship be fine? Her answer to both is no. That settles the loan. It doesn’t settle whether she helps in another way.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Noreen’s sheet, filled in.

  • My answer: No loan.
  • Why, for me (I don’t have to say all of it): It would come from my emergency savings, and $900 from last time is still open.
  • Help I’ll really give: Sit with Marla on Saturday and call 211 (a free US line that connects people to local help, including rent assistance) and go through any applications. A $200 grocery gift, not a loan, offered once.
  • The Clean Ask (what I’ll say): “I’ve thought about it, and I’m not going to lend the money. I’d like to help another way, if you’ll let me.”
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “After everything”: “I haven’t forgotten, and I’m grateful. My answer on the loan is the same.” “Just until next month”: “I hope things turn around soon. It’s still no on the loan.”
  • My No-Agreement Plan: If she keeps asking, I give the same answer in the same words and don’t add reasons.
  • The one thing I won’t do: Make up an excuse like “my money’s all tied up.”

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Noreen: “Marla, I’ve thought about what you asked. I’m not going to lend the money.”

Marla: “Noreen. I wouldn’t ask if I had any other choice.”

Noreen: “I know. I’m so sorry you’re in this spot. I’d like to help another way. Could we sit down Saturday and call 211 together? They can point you to rent help.”

Marla: “I don’t need a hotline. I need four thousand dollars.”

Noreen: “I understand. I can’t lend it. I’d also like to give you $200 for groceries. It’s a gift, not a loan.”

Marla: “After everything we’ve been through? I sat with you every day when Ernest was sick.”

Noreen: “You did, and I’ll never forget it. My answer on the loan is still the same.”

Marla: “I’ll pay it back next month. All of it.”

Noreen: “I hope things turn around soon. It’s still a no on the loan, especially with the $900 from last time still open.”

Marla: “Wow. Okay.”

Noreen: “My offer for Saturday stands. Ten o’clock?”

Marla: “I’ll think about it.”

Marla is hurt, and Noreen feels terrible. She didn’t invent an excuse, and she didn’t let thirty years of friendship be used as the price of the loan.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Marla says, “Okay. I get it.” Follow through on what you offered, on the day you said. Help you promised and then let slide does more damage than a clear no.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Marla accepts Saturday but asks, “Could you do $1,000 then?” That’s a new request, so answer it on its own terms. If you’ve already decided no, say so: “It’s no on any loan. The $200 is yours, and I’ll see you Saturday.”

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
Marla won’t accept the no. Friends start calling Noreen to say Marla is “really struggling” and “you’re the only one who can help.” This is group pressure (Chapter 27, Groups, Media, and Manufactured Pressure).

Try saying: “I care about Marla too. I’ve told her my answer, and I’ve offered to help another way. That’s between her and me.”

You don’t owe each caller a new explanation.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
Marla says she understands. A week later she texts: “Guess I found out who my real friends are. Rent’s due Friday.”

Try saying: “I’m still your friend, and I’m still sorry things are hard. My answer on the loan hasn’t changed. Saturday’s offer stands.”

Give the same answer in the same calm tone. Each new reason you add gives her one more thing to argue with.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html: “Marla, I know today was hard. I meant what I said: I can’t lend the money, and I’d really like to help with the rent assistance calls. I’m free Saturday at 10 and can come to you. The $200 is a gift, no strings.”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html:
Marla may stay angry for a while, or for good. That’s a real cost, and it’s hers to carry as much as yours. Noreen can keep the door open (“I miss you. Coffee whenever you’re ready”) without reopening the loan.

If anyone threatens you, or pressures you into handing over control of your money, accounts or cards, that’s no longer a loan request. Go to Chapter 11 and get help. The numbers to call are in the safety and support box at the start of this library. For questions about your own savings or retirement, talk to a qualified financial adviser.

parts.html:

  • Any earlier loan still open? $900 of $1,500.
  • If it never came back, would I be okay? No, it’s emergency savings.
  • Would the friendship be okay? Probably not.
  • My answer: No loan.
  • Help I’ll really give, and when: 211 calls together, Saturday at 10. $200 gift, offered once.
  • My one repeat line: “My answer on the loan is the same.”

playbooks.title: Asking for money you're owed

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html: Rosalind is thirty-six and a freelance photographer. She shot a catalog for Trevor, who owns a furniture store. She sent her $2,400 invoice on May 3, due in thirty days, on June 2. She’s sent two friendly emails. Trevor replied to one on June 20: “End of month, promise.” It’s now July 2, and nothing has arrived.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Rosalind knows what was agreed: her emailed quote says payment is due in thirty days, and the photos are licensed for the catalog once paid. She knows Trevor is using the photos. She doesn’t know whether his business is short of cash, disorganized, or simply putting her last.

Trevor decides when he pays. Rosalind decides whether she does more work for him, and how far she takes it. Her quote’s license terms are real. She can state them honestly as facts, not as threats.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Rosalind’s sheet, filled in.

  • What I’m owed: $2,400, due a month ago.
  • The record: Quote email (Apr 2), invoice (May 3), reminders (Jun 5, Jun 19), Trevor’s reply (Jun 20).
  • The Clean Ask: “The $2,400 invoice from May was due on June 2, a month ago. I’d like it paid in full by Friday, July 10. If that’s hard, I’m open to a short payment plan in writing.”
  • What I’d accept: Full payment by Friday, July 10, or three payments of $800, all by July 31.
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “Cash is tight”: “I understand. Let’s set a plan with dates.” “I wasn’t happy with some shots”: “You didn’t mention it before. What specifically? Payment for the delivered work is still due.”
  • My No-Agreement Plan: A final written notice with a date. Then small claims court, after checking my local rules. No new work for Trevor until this is settled. Deposits upfront for new clients.
  • The one thing I won’t do: Post about him online.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Rosalind: “Hi Trevor. I’m calling about the catalog invoice. It’s $2,400, due on June 2. I’d like to get it settled.”

Trevor: “Right, sorry. It’s been a crazy few weeks.”

Rosalind: “I understand. Can you pay it by Friday, July 10?”

Trevor: “Honestly, cash is tight until the fall sale.”

Rosalind: “Then let’s set a plan. Could you do $800 by Friday, July 10, $800 by Monday, July 20, and $800 by Friday, July 31?”

Trevor: “Could we do two payments in September?”

Rosalind: “That would push a bill that was due in June into September. I can do the three payments, all in July.”

Trevor: “Fine. Three payments.”

Rosalind: “Thanks. I’ll email the dates now. Could you reply to confirm?”

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Confirm the plan in writing and mark each payment as it arrives. Say thank you when the last one lands. You may want to work with them again.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Trevor confirms the plan but changes the first date to “next week.” Accept one small change if you like, and put it in writing. Repeated changes deserve attention. Check what changed, why, and whether the revised plan is realistic.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: Trevor now says some shots weren’t usable. Ask what specifically, and when he planned to raise it. If there’s a real problem, offer a fair fix. If it’s new and vague, say so calmly: “This is the first I’ve heard of it, and the photos are in your catalog. The invoice is still due.”

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
The second $800, due Monday, July 20, doesn’t arrive.

Try saying: “Hi Trevor, the second payment of $800 was due on July 20 and hasn’t arrived. Could you send it by Friday, July 24? If the plan isn’t working, let’s talk today rather than let it slide.”

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html: “Hi Trevor, thanks for the call. To confirm the plan for invoice #118 ($2,400): $800 by Friday, July 10, $800 by Monday, July 20, and $800 by Friday, July 31, by bank transfer as before. Please reply to confirm. Rosalind”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html:
Send one final written notice: the amount, the dates, and what you’ll do next, such as filing in small claims court. Say it only if you’ll do it. Rules and limits vary, so check your local court’s website. You can also decide the cost in time and stress is too high and let it go. That’s a fair choice too, as long as it’s your choice. Either way, change how you work: a deposit upfront and payment before final files go out.

When it’s a friend who owes you: the same steps apply, gentler. “I wanted to check on the $500 from March. When can you pay it back?” If they can’t pay all of it, agree a small amount with a date. If you decide to forgive it, tell them so, and let it go for real.

playbooks.title: A family favor that later becomes a debt

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Hal is fifty-five. Three years ago, between jobs, he and his wife lived rent-free for five months in a unit of his uncle Leon’s duplex. Nobody talked about repayment. Hal said, “I’ll make it up to you, I promise.”

Last year Leon, now seventy-eight, started asking Hal to “keep an eye on” the duplex. Now Hal finds tenants, handles repairs and collects rent, about six hours a week, unpaid. When Hal mentioned it was a lot, Leon said, “After what I did for you? Family doesn’t charge family.”

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
Leon decides about his property. Hal decides about his time. Hal knows the favor was real and generous, and that he made a promise, a vague one. He doesn’t know what Leon thinks fair repayment looks like, whether Leon can afford a property manager, or how long Leon expects this to go on.

In the language of Chapter 7, Guilt, Favors, and Hidden Debts, the five months were a favor. “I’ll make it up to you” turned part of it into a real but undefined promise. Running a rental for free, forever, was never agreed. Hal’s fair move is to honor the promise by defining it, not to deny it.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Hal’s sheet, filled in.

  • What I want: To keep my promise in a way with an end, and to stop managing the duplex every week.
  • What I owe, honestly: Gratitude, and a fair return for five months’ rent. A year of unpaid management is already a real return.
  • The Clean Ask: “I’m grateful for what you did, and I said I’d make it up to you. I’d like us to agree what that looks like. I’ll keep managing the duplex until December 31, and help you hire a property manager. After that, I’m happy to be the backup for emergencies.”
  • Other option I’d accept: Keep managing it for a monthly fee.
  • Likely pushback and my reply: “After what I did”: “I haven’t forgotten. That’s why I’ve done it for a year, and why I’ll help with the handover.” “Family doesn’t charge family”: “Then let’s agree when this ends, as family.”
  • My No-Agreement Plan: From January, I’ll handle only emergencies. I’ll give Leon a list of three local property managers and help with the first call.
  • The one thing I won’t do: List everything I’ve done for him as a counter-ledger.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Hal: “Uncle Leon, I want to talk about the duplex. I’m grateful for those five months. I said I’d make it up to you, and I meant it.”

Leon: “So what’s the problem?”

Hal: “Six hours a week is more than I can keep doing. I’d like us to agree on an end. I’ll run it through December, and help you hire a property manager.”

Leon: “A stranger? After what I did for you?”

Hal: “I haven’t forgotten. That’s why I’ve done it for a year, and why I want the handover done properly.”

Leon: “Family doesn’t charge family.”

Hal: “I’m not charging you. I’m saying when I’ll stop. After December I’ll still come for emergencies.”

Leon: “Managers cost money.”

Hal: “They do. If you’d rather I keep doing it, we could talk about a fee. Or I can find three managers and you compare prices.”

Leon: “Find the three. I’m not promising anything.”

Hal: “Fair. I’ll have names by the end of the month.”

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Write it down in a short message, and do the handover well. A clean finish turns the favor into a shared story instead of an open account.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Leon agrees to a manager but wants Hal to “keep collecting the rent, it’s only a few minutes.” Decide whether that’s true and whether you’ll do it, and put a date on it if you do.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: Leon refuses any manager or fee. Hal sticks to his plan. “I understand. From January, I’ll handle emergencies only. The list of managers is here when you want it.” If Leon’s health or memory makes it hard for him to manage his own affairs, that’s a family conversation and possibly a legal one. Talk to an elder law attorney before anyone takes over his finances.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html:
In February Leon calls every Saturday with “small things.” Then a cousin calls to say Hal “abandoned” him.

Try saying: “We agreed I’d stop at the end of December and handle emergencies. A dripping faucet isn’t one. Would you like me to call the manager for you?”

To the cousin: “I managed it for over a year and set up a manager. If you’d like to help Leon, I can send you the details.”

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html: “Uncle Leon, thanks for talking today. To confirm: I’ll keep running the duplex through December 31. By the end of this month I’ll bring you three property managers to compare. From January, I’ll be your backup for emergencies like leaks or no heat. Love, Hal”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Hal can’t make Leon hire anyone. He can decide what he does from January. He keeps his line, stays warm and visits for reasons other than repairs. Leon may grumble for months. The relationship has a better chance with a clear limit than with a resentment that grows every Saturday.

sections.title: Relationships and family
sections.intro: These five playbooks cover people you can’t easily replace: parents, siblings, in-laws, a partner and an ex. With family there is rarely a clean “take it or leave it,” so each playbook spends as much time on what happens after the conversation as on the conversation itself.

playbooks.title: A difficult parent

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Ines is fifty-two. She runs the front desk at a dental practice. Her mother, Estelle, is seventy-eight and lives forty minutes away.

Estelle calls most days at about six, just as Ines starts dinner. The calls follow a pattern. A comment about Ines’s weight or her house. A comparison with her brother, Vic, “who always makes time for me.” And when Ines tries to end the call, a sigh: “I won’t keep you. I know I’m not a priority.”

Visits are the same, only longer. Estelle expects Ines every Sunday until dinner. Last month Ines left at three. Her mother didn’t call for four days, then told Vic that Ines “has no time for her own mother anymore.”

Ines loves her mother and wants to keep seeing her. She just wants to stop bracing for every call. This playbook covers criticism, comparisons, guilt and limits on calls and visits.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What Ines knows. The facts: daily calls at dinnertime, the weight comments, the comparisons, four days of silence after she left early. And that her mother lives alone.

What she doesn’t know. Why her mother does it. Loneliness, worry and habit are all possible, but they’re guesses. Ines doesn’t need the answer to act. If you’ve wondered whether your parent is a narcissist, Chapter 6, A Bad Moment or a Pattern?, explains why you can judge the pattern without a label.

Who decides. Ines decides how often she calls, how long she stays and which topics she will discuss. Estelle decides how she responds. Vic has no say in Ines’s schedule, though Estelle may try to bring him in.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Ines

  • What I want a say in: how often we talk, how long Sunday visits last, and whether my weight is a topic.
  • The Clean Ask: “Mom, I’d like to change how we do calls. I’ll call you Monday, Wednesday and Friday at about 7:30, after dinner, so I can actually listen. I’ll keep coming for Sunday lunch and stay until about three. How does that sound to you?”
  • The second ask: “When my weight comes up, I’m going to change the subject.”
  • What she may say: “So I need an appointment now?” “Vic calls every day.” “I guess I’m a burden.” Silence.
  • The one thing I won’t do: argue about whether she’s critical, or list everything I do for her.
  • The No-Agreement Plan: I keep my schedule anyway. If she calls at six, I say, “I’m making dinner. I’ll call you at 7:30,” and I do. If my weight comes up twice in one call, I end the call kindly. If she goes quiet, I call at the usual time and keep it short.
  • Fairness check (The Four Fair Influence Tests): My reasons are true and the times are specific. She can be unhappy, and I won’t punish her with coldness. She is older and more alone than I am, so I’ll keep the calls warm and make sure she can reach me in an emergency.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Ines raises it on a Sunday, after lunch, with nobody else there.

Ines: “Mom, can I talk to you about our phone calls? Every day at dinnertime is too much for me. I’d like to call you Monday, Wednesday and Friday, around 7:30. Then I’m not stirring a pot with one hand while we talk.”

Estelle: “So now I need an appointment to talk to my own daughter.”

Ines: “Not an appointment. A time when you get my full attention.”

Estelle: “Vic calls me every day. He’s never too busy.”

Ines: “I’m glad he does. This is what works for me.”

Estelle: “Well. I suppose I’m just a burden.”

Ines: “You’re not a burden. I want to keep talking to you. I want it to be good when we do.”

Estelle: “And Sundays? Are you cutting those too?”

Ines: “I’ll come every Sunday. I’ll stay until about three. And one more thing. When you bring up my weight, I’m going to change the subject.”

Estelle: “I’m your mother. I’m allowed to worry.”

Ines: “You can worry. I’m still not going to discuss it. Tell me about the new neighbor.”

A long pause.

Estelle: “She parks on my side of the street.”

They talk about the neighbor. Estelle is cool for the rest of the visit. At three she says, “Drive safe,” and doesn’t walk Ines to the door. Nothing has been agreed. Ines has said it once, and that is enough for today.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Confirm it in one sentence, then be completely reliable for the first few weeks. Less contact feels safer when it’s predictable. Don’t add extra calls out of guilt, and when a call goes well, say so.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: She accepts the call times but not the topic limit, or she wants four calls a week. Trade where you honestly can: “I could add a short call on Saturday mornings.” Offer only what you’ll keep doing in six months. The weight topic needs no trade. A limit on your own behavior doesn’t need her permission.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
“I’ll call whenever I like.” She can. You decide when you answer. Use the same calm sentence each time: “I’m making dinner. I’ll call you at 7:30.” Then call at 7:30.

If she goes quiet for days, use Chapter 9, Silence, Distance, and Conditional Warmth: name it once, keep the door open, carry on. If Vic gets drawn in: “I changed the call times. I’m still calling three times a week and seeing her Sundays. All good.” Don’t ask him to take sides.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html: The daily calls start again, or she says, “I never agreed to that.” Don’t argue about who agreed. Go back to your part: “We said Monday, Wednesday and Friday. I’ll call you tonight at 7:30.” If you slip and pick up at six, go back to the plan the next day.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
Estelle hasn’t agreed to the schedule, so there is no agreed step to confirm yet. This message states Ines’s own next step.

“Thanks for lunch, Mom. I’ll call Monday around 7:30. Love you.”

Don’t reopen the discussion in the text.

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Then the question becomes “What contact do I want?” Chapter 28, When They Still Say No, sets out the paths. Ines might keep her schedule and let her mother grumble. If every call still turns to criticism, she might make calls shorter or fewer. Some readers will consider low contact or no contact. Each choice has real costs, only you can weigh them, and you can change your mind later. If a parent’s behavior involves threats, control of your money, or fear, go to Chapter 11, When Pressure Becomes Danger, before anything else. The numbers to call are in the safety and support box at the start of this library.

parts.heading: Worksheet: call and visit plan
parts.html:
Check first: Keep this somewhere private. If someone checks your phone or papers, keep the plan in your head.

Completed example: Ines

  • Calls: Monday, Wednesday, Friday, about 7:30 p.m., about 30 minutes.
  • Visits: Sunday lunch, leaving about 3.
  • Topics I’ll decline: my weight, my house.
  • My line for declining: “I’m not going to talk about that. Tell me about the neighbor.”
  • My line for comparisons: “I’m glad he’s doing well.”
  • My line for ending a call: “I need to go now. Love you. Talk Wednesday.”
  • If she goes quiet: I call at the usual time and keep it short.
  • Emergencies: She has my number and Vic’s. If she says it’s urgent, I answer any time.
  • Review date: first Sunday of next month.
