playbooks.title: Sharing care of an aging parent with siblings

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Bernard is sixty-one, a retired mail carrier. His father, Lionel, is eighty-six and lives ten minutes away. Since a fall in the spring, Lionel needs rides to appointments, groceries, his pills sorted each week, his prescriptions refilled, his house cleaned and his yard kept up.

In April, after the fall, the siblings divided the work. His sister, Rita, a nurse two hours away, agreed to manage refills. His brother, Cal, across the country, agreed to arrange paid help. Bernard kept the rides, the groceries, the weekly pill box and the yard. None of these tasks has an agreed backup. When a refill was missed and a cleaner canceled, Bernard covered both. He wants a family call that settles who checks completion and what happens when someone cannot do their part.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What Bernard knows. What slipped, and when. In May, the refill wasn’t ordered, and Lionel was down to two days of pills before Bernard noticed while sorting the box. In June, the cleaner canceled by text to Lionel’s phone, and nobody heard about it for a week. What Lionel wants: to stay in his house, keep his Thursday lunch with friends, and not have “strangers poking around.”

What he doesn’t know. Why each gap happened. Rita may have been on night shifts. The cleaning company may have been short of staff. He suspects Cal thinks booking the cleaner was the whole job. That’s a guess, so he’ll ask rather than assume.

Who decides. Lionel decides about his own life, as far as he is able. Decisions about his medical care belong to Lionel, his doctors and anyone he has legally named, and they are not made in a sibling call. Each sibling decides what they’ll take on, and Bernard decides what he’ll keep doing. Questions about legal authority over Lionel’s money go to an elder law attorney.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Bernard

  • Before the call: I wrote down the two gaps with their dates, and asked Dad what he’s comfortable having shared. No passwords or medical details.
  • What needs to change: Each essential task needs an agreed owner, a way to confirm completion, and a backup who has actually agreed. A name in a table is not enough.
  • The Clean Ask: “The plan we made in the spring mostly works. When an agreed task falls through, I keep becoming the backup. I need us to plan for those gaps. For refills and cleaning, can we agree who does it, how the rest of us will know it’s done, and who covers if that person can’t?”
  • Likely pushback: “It only happened once.” “I can’t control the cleaning company.” “You’re closest, so you’re the natural backup.” “Let’s not make this a big deal.”
  • The one thing I won’t do: turn this into who was the favorite growing up. Or quietly cover a missed task again without telling anyone.
  • The No-Agreement Plan: If we can’t agree on checks and backups by the end of the month, I’ll tell them which gaps I’ll cover in a real emergency and which I won’t, from what date. Before that date, Dad and I will ask the pharmacy what refill reminders or delivery it offers, and look for a second cleaning contact he’s comfortable with. I’ll ask an elder law attorney anything about authority. Nothing essential will be left uncovered.
  • Fairness check: specific tasks, no blame for the two gaps, no using Dad’s health to guilt anyone. Dad stays in charge of his own life.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
A video call on a Sunday evening in early July. The day before, Bernard sent a short note listing the two gaps and their dates.

Bernard: “Thanks for doing this. The plan we made in the spring mostly works. Two things slipped, the refill in May and the cleaner in June, and both times I filled in. I’m not blaming anyone. When an agreed task falls through, I keep becoming the backup. I need us to plan for those gaps.”

Rita: “May was me. I was on nights that week and it went right out of my head.”

Bernard: “Thanks for saying so. It could happen to any of us. That’s why I’d like each task to have three things: who does it, how the rest of us know it’s done, and who covers if that person can’t.”

Cal: “Isn’t that a lot of process for two slip-ups?”

Bernard: “Maybe. But both times, nobody knew until Dad was nearly out of pills or the house had gone three weeks without cleaning. I’d like us to find out sooner.”

Rita: “For refills, I can text the group once I’ve ordered them. That’s easy.”

Bernard: “That works. And if you’re on nights and can’t get to it?”

Rita: “Could you cover? You’re closest.”

Bernard: “I can, if you tell me by the 25th. What I can’t do is find out when Dad’s nearly out.”

Rita: “Fair. By the 25th.”

Cal: “The cleaning’s on me, but I can’t control when the company cancels.”

Bernard: “No. Could they email you when they cancel, and you rebook within the week? And could you call Dad on cleaning days, so you know it happened?”

Cal: “I’ll set up the emails. I already call him most Fridays, so I’ll ask then.”

Bernard: “Thank you. Who backs up the cleaning if the company can’t send anyone? I’d rather it wasn’t me by default.”

Rita: “The neighbor’s daughter cleans for a couple of people on Dad’s street. I could ask her.”

Bernard: “Would you ask her this week? Until she says yes, we don’t have a backup.”

A backup only counts once that person has agreed. Bernard says so out loud, so nobody leaves the call thinking the gap is covered.

Rita: “I’ll ask her Tuesday.”

Bernard: “Last one. I sort Dad’s pill box every Sunday. If I’m sick or away, who does it?”

Rita: “I can drive up for that. Give me a day’s notice.”

Bernard: “Thanks. I’ll keep next week’s box filled ahead, so a day’s notice is always enough.”

Refills and the pill box now have an owner, a check and a backup. Cleaning has an owner and a check, and its backup is still a question. That’s further than they were an hour ago, and Bernard is no longer the safety net nobody mentions.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Confirm the owners, checks and backups in writing the same day. Then let people do their tasks their own way. Taking a task back because it isn’t done your way puts you back where you started.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: That’s what happened here, and it’s the most common outcome. Take what’s agreed, name what’s still uncovered, and plan for it: paid help, a local service, or asking again in a month. When relatives offer ideas but not time, try: “Good idea. Can you set it up?”

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: “Just handle it if something slips.” That makes you the permanent backup without anyone saying so. You can decline: “I’ll cover a real emergency. For ordinary gaps, we need another plan.” Then put your No-Agreement Plan into action: tell them which gaps you’ll stop covering and when, and look at paid help or services with your parent, if they agree. In the US, your local Area Agency on Aging can point you to services such as meal delivery and respite care (short breaks for caregivers). Don’t leave an essential need uncovered to prove a point.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html: Two months later, the refill text doesn’t come, and neither does a message by the 25th. Remind Rita once, directly: “I didn’t see the refill text this month. Is it ordered?” If refills don’t work for her anymore, thank her, and agree a new owner and backup, rather than quietly taking the task back onto your own list. Tell everyone who is doing it now.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
Post it in the family chat that evening. Keep out account numbers, passwords and medical details.

“Thanks, both of you. Here’s what we agreed. Refills: Rita orders them and texts the group when it’s done. If she can’t, she tells me by the 25th and I’ll do it. Cleaning: Cal books it, gets the company’s cancellation emails and rebooks within the week, and checks with Dad on cleaning days. Cleaning backup: Rita asks the neighbor’s daughter on Tuesday, so that one isn’t settled yet. Pill box: I sort it on Sundays and keep next week’s filled ahead. If I’m sick or away, I give Rita a day’s notice and she fills it. Let’s check in on Sunday, August 2.”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Some siblings never take a share, or never take the checking seriously. You can’t make them. You can decide how much of the gap you’ll fill, and say so. Arrange the help you and your parent can afford, tell the family which ordinary gaps you won’t cover, and accept that the sharing may never be fair. Chapter 28, When They Still Say No, helps with the resentment. If your parent’s needs grow beyond what family can safely handle, talk to their doctor and qualified professionals.

playbooks.title: In-laws

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Colleen is thirty-eight. She and her husband, Pete, have two kids, aged six and nine. Pete’s parents, Rupert and Anita, live fifteen minutes away and have a key “for emergencies.”

Anita lets herself in on weekday mornings with muffins, and twice she has rearranged the kitchen cupboards. She comments on screen time in front of the kids. In October, she announced to the extended family that “everyone’s at our house for Christmas, as always,” before Colleen and Pete had talked about it.

Rupert and Anita are generous and love the kids, which makes this harder. Colleen and Pete want two things: a text before visits, and Christmas Day at home this year.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What they know. The facts above, and that Rupert and Anita help a lot with school pickups and sick days.

What they don’t know. How Rupert and Anita will take it. And the bigger unknown: whether Pete will hold the line when his mother is upset. That’s why the first conversation is between Colleen and Pete.

Who decides. Colleen and Pete decide who comes into their home and when, and where they spend Christmas. Rupert and Anita decide how they respond. As a general rule, each partner handles their own parents, so Pete speaks.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Colleen and Pete

  • First, our agreement: We both want a text before visits, with a yes from us before they come. Christmas Day at home; them for dinner on the 26th. Pete speaks. Colleen is there and backs him. We don’t blame each other in front of them.
  • The Clean Ask, from Pete: “Mom, Dad, we love having you so involved. We’d like you to text before you come over and wait for us to say yes. Mornings are hectic, and we need to know who’s coming. And we’re going to spend Christmas Day at home with the kids this year. We’d love you to come for dinner on the 26th.”
  • Likely pushback: “So we’re not welcome?” “This is Colleen’s idea.” “We’ve always done Christmas at our house.”
  • The one thing we won’t do: cut back their time with the kids to make a point. That would be punishment, not a limit.
  • The No-Agreement Plan: If they drop in anyway, Pete or Colleen says at the door, “We weren’t expecting you. Next time, text first.” If it keeps happening after two reminders, we’ll ask for the key back and keep a spare with a neighbor. We’ll spend Christmas Day at home whether they agree or not.
  • Fairness check: Real reasons, a specific ask, and they can be unhappy without being punished.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
At Rupert and Anita’s house, after Sunday lunch. The kids are outside.

Pete: “Mom, Dad, can we talk about a couple of things? We’ve talked about it together, and we want to ask you both.”

Anita: “That sounds serious.”

Pete: “It isn’t bad. We love how much you help. We’d like you to text before coming over and wait for a yes. Mornings are chaos, and we need to know who’s coming.”

Anita: “So we’re not welcome anymore.”

Pete: “You’re very welcome. We’re asking you to text first, not to stop coming.”

Rupert: “This is Colleen’s idea. You never minded before, son.”

Rupert attributes the decision to Colleen. Pete makes their shared position clear.

Pete: “It’s our idea, together. I should have said something sooner.”

Colleen: “We both want this. And we love the muffins.”

Anita: “Fine. I’ll text. Like a stranger.”

Pete: “Thank you. One more thing. We’re going to spend Christmas Day at home this year, just us and the kids. We’d love you to come for dinner on the 26th.”

Anita: “We’ve always done Christmas here. I’ve already told everyone.”

Pete: “I know. I’m sorry we didn’t talk sooner. This year we want the morning at home. The 26th is yours, if you’ll come.”

Anita: “I need to think about it.”

Pete: “Okay. Let us know by the first of December so we can plan.”

They agreed to text. Christmas is unsettled. Anita is hurt, and the drive home is quiet.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Thank them, and make it easy to keep. Reply quickly, and say yes often when it suits you. Answer honestly when you can. A text-first rule gives you room to say yes, suggest another time or decline.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Here, they agreed to text but not to Christmas. Hold what was agreed, and leave the rest with a date. If they decline the 26th, that’s their choice; you don’t need to change your plan. Keep inviting them to ordinary things, so the limit doesn’t turn into distance.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: “We’re family. We don’t need permission.” Pete: “I hear you. We’re still asking for a text first.” Then act on your plan. You can take the muffins at the door and still not invite them in. After two reminders, ask for the key back, with one sentence of reason and no lecture.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html: Three weeks later Anita lets herself in “just to drop off soup.” Pete calls that evening: “Thanks for the soup, Mom. We said you’d text first. Please do that next time.” One calm reminder from the right person usually does more than a second big talk. If Pete won’t give the reminders, the real conversation is with Pete. Chapter 25, Dating, Intimacy, and Difficult Relationships, covers how to have it as equals.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
From Pete, in the family chat or a text to both parents:

“Thanks for listening today. We know it wasn’t easy to hear. So: a text before coming over, and we’ll answer quickly. Christmas dinner here on the 26th at 4, if you can come. Let us know by December 1.”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Some in-laws keep testing a limit. You can still keep it, as a couple, without a fight each time, perhaps by seeing them more at their house and less at yours. If your own parent is the one crossing lines, swap the roles in this playbook: you speak, your partner backs you. If in-law behavior involves threats, control of money, or fear, go to Chapter 11, When Pressure Becomes Danger. The numbers to call are in the safety and support box at the start of this library.

parts.html:
Check first: Fill this in together, as a couple. Keep it somewhere private, not on a shared family device or account.

  • What we’re offering: dinner on the 26th; quick replies to texts; their usual school pickups stay the same.
  • Who speaks: Pete. Colleen backs him.
  • Our exact words: “We’d like you to text before you come over and wait for us to say yes.”
  • If they say it’s one partner’s idea: “It’s our idea, together.”
  • If they drop in anyway: “We weren’t expecting you. Next time, please text first.”
  • After two reminders: we ask for the key back.
  • What we won’t do: blame each other in front of them; cut their time with the kids to punish them.
  • Check-in date (just us): January 10.

playbooks.title: The recurring fight with a partner

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Fred is forty-seven. He and Nell have been married fifteen years. They have the same fight about every three weeks.

It’s about weekends. Nell fills Saturdays with barbecues, dinners and birthday parties. Fred goes along, then gets quiet and short by mid-afternoon. Nell notices and says, “If you didn’t want to come, you should have said so.” Fred says, “I never get a say.” Nell says, “Fine. Stay home next time.” It ends with a cold evening.

The surface topic moves around, but the shape stays the same. Fred wants to talk about the pattern, once, at a calm time, instead of having round twenty.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What Fred knows. His part: he agrees to plans, then sulks. And what the fight is about for him: no say in his own time off.

What he doesn’t know. What it’s about for Nell. He suspects she feels she carries all the work of keeping friends and family close. That’s a guess, and he’ll ask instead of telling her.

Who decides. In a partnership, nobody is the boss. They decide shared plans together, and each decides about their own time. Fred can’t make Nell plan less. He can change how he says yes and no.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Fred

  • Timing: a weeknight after the kids are in bed. Not during or right after the fight.
  • What I’ll own first: going along with plans and then sulking. That isn’t fair to her.
  • The Clean Ask: “I’d like us to try one change for a month. One Saturday a month with nothing planned, so I have some say over my own time. And I want to hear what this fight is about for you.”
  • What I’ll offer: to plan one social thing a month myself, start to finish.
  • Likely pushback: “Just stop sulking.” “If I didn’t plan things, we’d never see anyone.” “Don’t analyze me.”
  • The one thing I won’t do: bring up past examples (“Last month at your sister’s…”).
  • The No-Agreement Plan: I stop the sulking anyway. When I don’t want to go, I say so when the plan is made, not at 3 p.m. If we keep getting stuck, I’ll suggest couples counseling, if we both want it.
  • Fairness check: I’m not using coldness to get my way. That’s what the sulking was.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Fred: “Can we talk about the weekend fight? Not to have it again. I’d like to try something different.”

Nell: “We don’t need to talk about it. Just stop sulking.”

Fred: “That’s fair. I go along with plans, then I sulk. That isn’t fair to you, and I want to stop.”

Nell: “Okay.” She sounds surprised.

Fred: “For me, the fight is about having no say in my own time off. Most Saturdays are planned before I know about them.”

Nell: “Because if I didn’t plan anything, we’d never see anyone. You never invite people over. Not once.”

Fred: “So for you it’s more about doing all the work of keeping us connected?”

Nell: “Yes. And then you act like I’m dragging you somewhere.”

Fred: “I didn’t see it that way. I’m sorry. Could we try something for a month? One Saturday a month with nothing planned. And I’ll plan one thing a month myself, people over or an outing. All of it, not just showing up.”

Nell: “You said you’d plan our anniversary dinner last year. I ended up booking it.”

That stings, and it’s true. Fred doesn’t defend himself.

Fred: “You’re right. If I drop it, tell me, and I’ll fix it.”

Nell: “Which Saturday?”

Fred: “First Saturday of the month?”

Nell: “Not in March. My sister’s birthday is that weekend.”

Fred: “Second Saturday in March, first from April?”

Nell: “Fine. We’ll see if you plan something.”

It isn’t warm. It’s a trial, with a doubt attached. That’s a fair place to start.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Write the trial down and keep your side early. Trust grows fastest when the person who was doubted delivers first. Check in after a month: “How did that feel for you?”

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Nell might agree to the free Saturday but say, “I don’t need you to plan things. I need you not to sulk.” Take that seriously. She’s telling you what matters most to her.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
“Don’t try to therapy me.” Drop the method and keep the goal: “Fair enough. I’m just tired of this fight. If you’ve got a better way, I’m in.” Then do your part anyway: stop sulking, and say “I’d rather not go” when the plan is made. Changing your own side often changes the fight.

If you’re met with contempt, mockery or punishment every time you raise something, Chapter 6, A Bad Moment or a Pattern?, helps you look at it clearly. If there is fear, threats or control, go to Chapter 11, When Pressure Becomes Danger.

Safety and support: If you feel afraid of your partner, scripts and joint counseling are not the answer. Read Chapter 11 and talk to an advocate privately. In the US, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788, from a device your partner can’t access. In immediate danger, call 911.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html: Nell books the free Saturday for a friend’s party. Raise it early and lightly: “That was our free Saturday. Can we move it to the next one?” If you slip and start sulking, own it quickly: “I’m doing the thing. I’m sorry. I’ll go and enjoy it, or I’ll stay home. I won’t sulk.” When the old fight starts, either of you can say, “I think we’re in the old fight. Can we stop and come back to it tonight?”

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
The next day, as a text or a calendar note:

“Thanks for last night. Trial for a month: second Saturday in March is free, then the first Saturday from April. I’m planning one thing a month, starting with dinner with friends this month. Check in April 15?”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Couples counseling can help with ordinary conflict if both people want it. If one person won’t go, a counselor on your own can still help. And many couples live well with a difference they’ve stopped fighting about. Where there is fear or control, don’t try joint counseling first. Get private help from an advocate, and read Chapter 11.

  • How it usually starts: a plan is made without me; I agree; I go quiet by mid-afternoon.

  • What it’s about for me: having no say in my own time off.
  • What it’s about for them (their words, not my guess): “I do all the work of keeping us connected.”
  • My part, honestly: going along, then sulking.
  • Trial change for me: plan one thing a month; say no when the plan is made.
  • Trial change we agreed together: one free Saturday a month.

playbooks.title: An ex who keeps reopening practical agreements

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Mara is forty-four. She and Dale split up fourteen months ago. They have no children together. In March, they agreed by email on the practical things. Dale would collect his boxes, tools and two bikes from Mara’s garage by the end of April. Their dog, Biscuit, would live with Mara. Dale would have Biscuit every other Saturday, 10 to 5, with handovers at the park by the library.

It’s now June. Most of Dale’s things are still in the garage. He texts the night before to change handover times. Twice he has shown up at Mara’s house without warning “to grab a drill.” Last week he wrote, “We never agreed you keep Biscuit,” followed by three long messages about what went wrong between them.

Mara isn’t afraid of Dale. She’s worn out. This playbook covers practical communication with an ex: belongings, handovers and agreed arrangements. If you share children, see the co-parenting box after the conversation.

Check first: If you feel afraid of your ex, if there have been threats, or if they follow you, monitor your phone or show up in ways that scare you, this playbook is not enough. Go to Chapter 11, When Pressure Becomes Danger, and talk to a domestic violence advocate before you change anything, from a device your ex can’t access. In the US, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788. A sudden change in how you respond can raise the risk. In immediate danger, call 911.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What Mara knows. What was agreed, because it’s in an email. What has happened since, with dates.

What she doesn’t know. Why Dale keeps reopening things: unhappy with the deal, disorganized, still hurt, or testing her. Also what the law says about anything they truly disagree on, such as who owns the dog. That’s a question for a family lawyer, not a text thread.

Who decides. Mara decides when her home is open, how she replies, and what she’s willing to renegotiate. Dale decides what he does. Neither of them can settle a legal dispute by text.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Mara

  • What was agreed, and where it’s written: March 12 email. Boxes, tools and bikes collected by April 30. Biscuit lives with me; Dale has him every other Saturday, 10 to 5, library park.
  • The Clean Ask, in writing: “I’d like us to stick to what we agreed in March. Your things need to be collected. I’m home this Saturday or next, 10 to noon. Which works? If you want to change anything about Biscuit, please send me a proposal in writing and I’ll think about it.”
  • My rule for messages: I answer the practical part. I don’t answer the rest.
  • Likely pushback: “I’ll come when I can.” “We never agreed about Biscuit.” Messages about the past. “You always need it in writing.”
  • The one thing I won’t do: argue about the relationship, or defend myself against digs.
  • The No-Agreement Plan: If his things aren’t collected by June 30, I’ll send one message with a final date, and ask a family lawyer what I’m allowed to do with anything left behind. I’ll keep the Biscuit schedule as written, and take any dispute to a lawyer, not a text thread. If he drops in without notice, I’ll say, “Saturday, 10 to noon,” and close the door.
  • Fairness check: I’m not using his things or Biscuit as leverage. I’m keeping to the agreement we both made.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
By text, because that’s where these exchanges happen.

Mara: “Your boxes, tools and bikes are still in my garage. Our March agreement was April 30. I’m home this Saturday or next Saturday, 10 to noon. Which works?”

Dale: “Can’t do Saturday. I’ll swing by Thursday night.”

Mara: “Thursday night doesn’t work for me. This Saturday or next, 10 to noon.”

Dale: “It’s half my stuff in there. I’ll come when I can.”

Mara: “I’ll be home Saturday 10 to noon to open the garage.”

Dale: “Also, I’ve been thinking. Biscuit should be with me half the week. We never agreed you keep him.”

Mara: “Our March 12 email says Biscuit lives with me and is with you every other Saturday, 10 to 5. If you’d like to propose a change, send it in writing and I’ll think about it.”

Dale: “Typical. Everything has to be in writing with you. That’s half of why we didn’t work.”

Mara doesn’t answer this one. There’s nothing practical in it.

Dale: “Fine. Saturday at 11.”

Mara: “Saturday at 11. See you then.”

On Saturday, Dale takes the boxes and leaves the tool chest and bikes: “No room in the truck.” It’s progress, not an ending.

Check first: if you share children. The same rules apply, with a few more. Keep handovers at the agreed times and places. Keep messages about the children’s practical needs. Never ask your children to carry messages or choose between you. For anything about a parenting plan, a court order, or a change to custody or support, talk to a family lawyer. Ask whether mediation suits your situation, especially if there has been fear or control. If your lawyer suggests a co-parenting app, it can keep messages in one place, though it can’t make the other person fair. Chapter 25, Dating, Intimacy, and Difficult Relationships, covers co-parenting messages in more detail.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Confirm in one line, show up on time, and thank them briefly. Don’t use a good handover to reopen anything else. A calm, boring arrangement is the goal.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Like Dale, they do part of it. Acknowledge what was done and name the next step, with a date: “Thanks for taking the boxes. The tool chest and bikes are still here. Can you collect them on the 21st between 10 and noon?” Keep each message to one practical matter.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: “I’m not coming on your schedule.” Answer once with the facts and your offer, then stop. If belongings stay put, follow your No-Agreement Plan, and ask a family lawyer before you move, sell or throw out anything. If they turn up without warning, you don’t have to open the door: “Not today. Saturday 10 to noon.” If turning up keeps happening or starts to scare you, go back to the safety box at the top of this playbook.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html: “I never agreed to Saturdays.” Point to the written version, once, without heat: “Our March 12 email says every other Saturday, 10 to 5. I’ll be at the park at 10.” Then do what you said. You don’t need to win the argument. Keep acting on the written version, and take any real dispute to a lawyer.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
After each handover or pickup, send one short confirmation.

“Thanks for collecting the boxes today. The tool chest and two bikes are still here. I’m home June 21, 10 to noon, if you’d like to pick them up then.”

Check first: Keep a copy of the agreement and your messages somewhere your ex can’t reach: not a shared cloud account, a shared computer, or a phone they know the code to. If you shared passwords during the relationship, think about whether your ex could still be watching your accounts before you change them. If that’s possible, talk to an advocate first.

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Your choices are the four in Chapter 28, When They Still Say No. Accept a small loose end. Escalate through a family lawyer or mediation if the stakes are real. Step back, with fewer messages and set times for replies. Or close it out, such as a final collection date set through a lawyer. You don’t have to keep renegotiating because the other person wants to.

sections.title: Endings and transitions
sections.intro: These five playbooks cover moments of change: repairing a harm, asking for room, ending a relationship, considering reopening one, and stepping out of a role. Each depends more on being clear with yourself first than on perfect words.

playbooks.title: The apology and repair

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Quentin is fifty-six. At his daughter Lena’s thirtieth birthday dinner, in front of her friends, he raised his glass and said, “Thirty, and still working out what she wants to be. At least the bakery taught her what not to do.” A few people laughed. Lena didn’t. Her bakery had closed the year before.

The next morning he texted: “Sorry if you took it the wrong way. You know I’m proud of you.” Lena replied, “Ok.” Her texts have been one line long ever since.

Quentin knows the text made it worse. This playbook is for when you are the one who caused the hurt.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What Quentin knows. Exactly what he said, where, and in front of whom. That his first apology put the problem in her feelings (“if you took it the wrong way”). That her replies have been short since.

What he doesn’t know. How it landed for her. Whether there’s older hurt behind it, from other jokes at other dinners. He can guess. He’ll ask.

Who decides. Quentin decides what he says and what he does from now on. Lena decides whether to accept the apology, when, and how close she wants to be. He can’t decide that for her, and asking her to hurry is a kind of pressure.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Quentin

  • What I did, in plain facts: made a joke about her bakery closing, at her birthday dinner, in front of her friends. Then sent an apology that blamed her reaction.
  • How it may have landed (my guess, to check with her): embarrassed in front of friends, and like I think she’s failed.
  • The Clean Ask: “Could we get coffee this week? I owe you a proper apology, not the text I sent.”
  • One thing I’ll do differently: no jokes about her work, her money or the bakery. Not in private, not in public.
  • What I won’t say: “but,” “I was only joking,” “you know how I am,” “are we good?”
  • The No-Agreement Plan: If she isn’t ready to meet, I’ll write the apology in a short message instead, say the door is open, and keep my promise anyway. I won’t chase her for a reply.
  • Fairness check: I’m apologizing because I was wrong, not to end my own discomfort or to get something back.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Saturday morning, a coffee shop near Lena’s apartment.

Quentin: “Thanks for coming. I owe you a real apology. The text I sent wasn’t one.”

Lena: “It’s fine, Dad.”

Quentin: “It isn’t. At your birthday, I made a joke about the bakery in front of your friends. It was unkind, and it was your night. Then I texted as if the problem was how you took it. The problem was what I said.”

Lena: “You always do this. Every family thing, there’s a dig.”

Quentin: “You’re right that it isn’t the first time. How did it land for you, that night?”

Lena: “Like you think I’m a failure. In front of people I’d just told about my new job.”

Quentin: “I’m sorry. I don’t think that. And I can see why you’d hear it.”

Lena: “And Thanksgiving, when you told Uncle Otis I’d ‘burned through my savings’?”

Quentin: “That matters too. I’d like to hear about it, today or another time.”

Lena: “Another time.”

Quentin: “Okay. Here’s what I’ll do. No more jokes about your work, your money or the bakery. Not in private, not in front of anyone.”

Lena: “I don’t know if I believe that.”

Quentin: “You don’t have to. I’d rather show you.”

Lena: “Okay. Thanks for saying it properly.”

She leaves a little early. It’s polite, not warm, and that’s a realistic first step.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Thank them and stop talking about it. Don’t ask, “So we’re good?” Keep the promise, starting this week. What follows an apology is what makes it last.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Lena accepted the apology but not the promise. That’s fair; trust comes back through behavior, not on request. If older hurts come up, offer a separate conversation and mean it.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: “I’m not ready to talk about it.” Respect that. “Okay. I’m sorry, and when you want to talk, I’m here.” If it feels right, send the apology in a short written message so they can read it in their own time. Then stop. Repeating the apology to get a response turns it into pressure.

parts.heading: If the hurt comes up again
parts.html:
Weeks later, Lena may bring up the birthday again. That doesn’t mean she has taken back her forgiveness or is being unfair. Hurt often comes back in waves. Listen for anything you haven’t addressed yet, and don’t answer with “I already apologized.”

A different thing happens if the old wrong is used to settle a new question, such as, “You admitted you were wrong, so you owe me whatever I ask.” You can own the past and still answer today’s question on its own terms: “I was wrong about what I said at your birthday. That doesn’t change my answer about this.”

If you are the one who slips, own it fast and briefly: “I just did it again. I’m sorry. That’s not what I promised.”

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
“Thanks for meeting me today. I meant what I said. I’d still like to hear about Thanksgiving whenever you want to talk about it.”

Keep it to that. The real follow-up is the next family dinner, with no jokes about her work.

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: You can’t force forgiveness. Keep the promise anyway, keep ordinary contact if it’s welcome, and give it time. If they’ve asked for no contact, respect that, and don’t go through relatives. Chapter 28, When They Still Say No, covers accepting a no you don’t like. And apologize only for real wrongs. If someone wants an apology for a fair limit you set, Chapter 30, Power Without Becoming What You Resent, explains how to repair the way you said it while keeping the limit.

parts.heading: Worksheet: repair plan
parts.html:
Check first: This is for you. Keep it private, and don’t hand it to the other person.

  • What I did (facts only): joke about the bakery at her birthday dinner, in front of friends; then an apology that blamed her reaction.
  • How it may have landed (my guess): embarrassed, and like I think she’s failed.
  • What they told me: “Like you think I’m a failure.”
  • Words I’ll avoid: “but,” “only joking,” “are we good?”
  • One thing I’ll do differently: no jokes about her work, money or the bakery.
  • How they’ll see it: at Sunday dinners and family events.
  • If they aren’t ready: one short written apology, then no chasing.
  • Older hurts to come back to: Thanksgiving comment to Uncle Otis.

playbooks.title: Asking for space

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Hollis is forty-one. She and Arlo have been together three years and live in separate apartments. Her father died three months ago. She’s handling his paperwork, working full time, and sleeping badly.

Arlo wants to help. He comes over most evenings, texts through the day to check on her, and plans their weekends. Hollis is grateful, and she’s exhausted. She wants two weeks with fewer visits and quieter evenings. She isn’t ending anything. She’s afraid that “I need space” will sound as if she is.

The same shape works for space from a friend or a family member. If you want space from someone because you’re afraid of them, this isn’t the right playbook. Go to Chapter 11, When Pressure Becomes Danger. The numbers to call are in the safety and support box at the start of this library.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What Hollis knows. What she needs: fewer evenings together, fewer daytime texts, for about two weeks. Why: grief and tiredness. That she wants to stay with Arlo.

What she doesn’t know. How Arlo will hear it. He may fear she’s pulling away; that’s a guess. She also doesn’t know for sure that two weeks will be enough. She’ll say so honestly.

Who decides. Hollis decides how she spends her evenings. Arlo decides how he feels about it and whether the arrangement works for him. The shape of the break is something they decide together.

Check first: Be honest with yourself. Is this a pause, or a slow way of leaving? If you’ve already decided to end things, asking for space isn’t fair to them. Use Playbook 18 instead.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Hollis

  • What space means, specifically: two weeks. See each other Wednesday and Saturday. Texts in the evening, not all day. A call any night either of us needs one.
  • The Clean Ask: “For the next two weeks, could we see each other Wednesday and Saturday instead of most nights, and text in the evenings? Since Dad died I’m running on empty, and I need some quiet. I’m not ending anything. Can we have dinner on the 22nd and talk about how it went?”
  • Likely pushback: “Are you breaking up with me?” “Is there someone else?” “Let me help, I’ll bring dinner.” “If you need space, maybe we’re done.”
  • The one thing I won’t do: go quiet without explaining, or promise more certainty than I have.
  • The No-Agreement Plan: I’ll still take the quiet evenings. I’ll offer the two weekly dates, evening texts and dinner on the 22nd, but those plans need his agreement too. If he declines them, I’ll respect that and decide what contact I can offer next.
  • Fairness check: I’m not using distance as punishment. I’m telling him exactly what I’m asking for and for how long.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Hollis: “Can I ask you for something? I’ll say up front: I’m not ending things. For the next two weeks, I’d like us to see each other Wednesday and Saturday instead of most nights. And text in the evenings, not through the day. I’m worn out since Dad died. I need some quiet.”

Arlo: “Is this you breaking up with me slowly?”

Hollis: “No. If it were, I’d tell you. This is about being tired, not about us.”

Arlo: “Is there someone else?”

Hollis: “No. There’s nobody else.”

Arlo: “I just want to help. I could bring dinner and leave.”

Hollis: “I know you do, and you have helped. Right now, help looks like quiet.”

Arlo: “Two weeks feels like a long time.”

Hollis: “We’d still see each other twice a week and talk every evening. Can we have dinner on the 22nd and talk about how it went for both of us?”

Arlo: “Okay. Can I at least text if I’m worried?”

Hollis: “Yes. I’ll answer that night.”

Arlo: “Fine. I don’t love it.”

Hollis: “I know. Thank you.”

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Keep your side exactly: the evening texts, Wednesday and Saturday, dinner on the 22nd. Small promises kept during a break show it really is a pause.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Arlo might say, “One week, not two,” or “Fewer visits, but I need to hear from you at lunch.” If you can honestly agree, trade: “A quick text at lunch is fine. I’d still like two weeks.” Don’t agree to something you’ll resent by day three.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: “If you need space from me, maybe we should just break up.” This may come from hurt, or it may be used as an ultimatum. You can keep your limit, and they can decide whether to stay in the relationship. “I don’t want that. I’m asking for two weeks, not an ending. If you need time to think about what it means for you, I understand.” Then take the space you asked for, kindly.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html: On Tuesday he turns up with dinner “just for ten minutes,” or the daytime texts start again. Be kind and clear: “Thank you. I meant what I asked for. I’ll see you tomorrow.” If you’re the one tempted to cancel the dinner on the 22nd, don’t. Keeping the date is what makes the space safe for both of you.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html: “Thanks for hearing me tonight. So: Wednesday and Saturday, texts in the evening, and dinner on the 22nd at the Thai place at 7. Talk tomorrow night.”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: You can’t make someone comfortable with a pause. If asking for space ends it for them, that’s their choice, and painful. You decide whether the room you need is worth that risk. If two weeks keeps turning into “I still need more,” that tells you something too, and the real question may be Playbook 18’s. Grief is heavy. Talk to a friend or a counselor if it isn’t easing. If you ever feel life isn’t worth living, call or text 988, the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

parts.heading: Worksheet: space agreement
parts.html:
Check first: Keep your preparation notes private. Share only the terms you want to discuss.

Completed example: Hollis

  • What I’m asking for: see each other Wednesday and Saturday; texts in the evening.
  • For how long: two weeks, until the 22nd.
  • What stays the same: we’re together; calls any night either of us needs one.
  • Why, in one sentence: “Since Dad died I’m running on empty, and I need some quiet.”
  • What I’m not sure about (said honestly): whether two weeks will be enough.
  • Return date and place: dinner on the 22nd, 7 p.m.
  • What I’ll do if they can’t accept it: keep my side and talk honestly on the 22nd.

playbooks.title: Ending a relationship

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Tamsin is fifty. She and Desmond have been together seven years and share a rented apartment, with both their names on the lease. For about a year, Tamsin has known they want different lives. Desmond wants to retire to Florida in two years. Tamsin wants to stay near her grandchildren. They tried counseling for six months. It helped them talk. It didn’t change what each of them wants.

She has decided to end the relationship. She has never been afraid of Desmond. She is afraid of the conversation.

Ending a long friendship follows the same shape, with fewer practical steps. Often a friendship can simply fade; say it directly when they ask, or when a fade would leave them confused.

Check first: If you have any reason to fear how the other person will react, don’t do this alone in private. Tell someone you trust, plan a safer way, and talk to a domestic violence advocate first. In the US, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788. Chapter 11, When Pressure Becomes Danger, explains why leaving can be a risky time. In immediate danger, call 911.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What Tamsin knows. Her decision, her main reason, and that she can stay with her sister for now.

What she doesn’t know. How Desmond will react, and how the lease and shared things will be sorted out. Her position on the lease is a question for a lawyer or the landlord, not for the first conversation.

Who decides. Tamsin decides whether she stays in the relationship. That doesn’t need Desmond’s agreement. Desmond decides how he responds. Practical matters, such as who stays in the apartment and who keeps what, they decide together, with legal advice where needed.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Tamsin

  • Am I sure? Yes. I’ve thought about it for a year, and we tried counseling. I’m not deciding because of one bad week.
  • Where and when: at home, on a Thursday evening, with no plans the next day. Not before a holiday or his birthday.
  • My decision, in the first minute: “I’ve decided to end our relationship.”
  • My one honest reason: “We want different lives. You want Florida, and I want to stay near the grandkids. I don’t think either of us should give that up.”
  • My repeat line: “I hear you. I’m not going to change my mind. I’m sorry.”
  • The Clean Ask, for practical things only: “Can we talk about the practical things on Saturday, once we’ve both had some time?”
  • Tonight: I’ll stay at my sister’s. My bag is packed. I’ll call my friend Pat afterward.
  • The No-Agreement Plan: The relationship is over whether or not he agrees. If we can’t agree on practical matters, I’ll get legal advice about the lease and keep all practical messages short and in writing.
  • Fairness check: I won’t soften it into “a break” if I’ve decided. I won’t hint I might change my mind.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Tamsin: “Desmond, I need to talk to you about us. This is hard to say. I’ve decided to end our relationship.”

Desmond: “What? Where is this coming from?”

Tamsin: “We want different lives. You want Florida, and I want to stay near the grandkids. I’ve thought about it for a long time, and I don’t think either of us should give that up.”

Desmond: “Then let’s go back to counseling. We stopped too soon.”

Tamsin: “I’ve thought about that. Counseling helped us talk. It didn’t change what we each want. I’m past the point where I think more would help.”

Desmond: “Tell me what I did. I’ll change it.”

Tamsin: “It isn’t something you did wrong. It’s that I know this isn’t the right life for me.”

Desmond: “Seven years, and you’re just done?”

Tamsin: “I know how much these years mean. They mean a lot to me too. I’m not going to change my mind. I’m sorry.”

Desmond: “I think you’re making a mistake.”

Tamsin: “Maybe I’ll have hard days. I’m still sure. I’m going to stay at my sister’s tonight. Can we talk about the practical things on Saturday?”

Desmond: “I don’t want to talk about practical things.”

Tamsin: “Okay. Saturday, if you’re ready. I’m not going to disappear on you.”

She leaves. Desmond is crying and angry. She cries in the car, then calls Pat.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Sometimes the other person says, “I’ve felt it too.” Don’t rush the practical side while things feel friendly. Talk practical things on a set day, put agreements in writing, and get advice on anything legal.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: “Okay, it’s over, but let’s keep living together until spring.” Or “Let’s stay friends right away.” Or “Let’s just take a break.” Only agree to what you’d still accept in a month. Living together can work for a short, set time, with clear rules. Friendship, if it comes, usually comes after distance. Don’t accept “a break” if you’ve decided.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html:
“I’m not accepting this.” You don’t need their acceptance. Repeat once: “I hear you. My decision is made.” Keep practical contact short and in writing. If refusal turns into following you, turning up uninvited, monitoring your phone, or threats, that’s no longer a disagreement. Go to Chapter 11 and get help.

If they say they might hurt themselves, take it seriously. In the US, call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or 911 if they’re in immediate danger. Ask whether there’s someone who can be with them. Their safety matters. It still doesn’t mean you have to stay.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html: They seem to accept it, then the late-night calls start: “Can we talk one more time?” You can say, “I’ll talk about practical things on Saturday. I’m not going to reopen the decision.” If you’re the one wavering out of guilt, don’t send mixed signals. Comfort that hints at a way back feels kind now and is cruel later.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
After the practical talk, confirm it in writing:

“Thanks for talking on Saturday. Here’s what we agreed. You’ll stay in the apartment through March. I’ll collect my things on Sundays, 1 to 4, and text first. We’ll each call the landlord this week about the lease. Anything else, let’s put in writing.”

Check first: Keep copies of messages and agreements somewhere the other person can’t reach. Before changing passwords or shared accounts, think about whether they could be watching. If that’s possible, talk to an advocate first, from a safe device.

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: The ending itself needs no agreement. On practical matters, get legal advice for anything involving a lease, property, money or children, and ask whether mediation suits your situation, especially if there has been fear or control. Chapter 29, Your Next Chapter Starts Here, covers what comes after.

parts.heading: Worksheet: ending plan
parts.html:
Check first: Keep this where the other person can’t find it. If someone checks your phone or papers, keep it in your head.

  • My one-sentence reason: we want different lives.
  • My repeat line: “I’m not going to change my mind. I’m sorry.”
  • Where I’ll stay tonight: my sister’s.
  • Who I’ll call afterward: Pat.
  • Practical list: keys, my belongings, shared bills, the lease, streaming and phone accounts.
  • Questions for a lawyer or the landlord: how to come off the lease; what happens to the deposit.
  • Practical talk: Saturday.

playbooks.title: Considering reconnection

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Earl is sixty-six, a retired bus mechanic. He hasn’t spoken to his younger sister, Opal, in nine years. After their mother’s funeral they argued about who had done more for her at the end. Earl said Opal had “abandoned” their mother. He knew as he said it that it wasn’t fair.

Last month a cousin mentioned that Opal had surgery. Earl has been thinking about her ever since. He isn’t sure whether to reach out, or what he’d say.

This playbook is about considering reconnection with estranged family or an ex. The first half of the work is deciding whether to reach out at all. It will not help you win someone back. If someone ended a relationship with you, their decision stands. Reconnection here means honest contact on terms both people choose.

Check first: If the distance began because someone hurt you, threatened you or controlled you, you don’t owe them reconnection. Talk it through with a counselor first, and read Chapter 11, When Pressure Becomes Danger. If the other person chose distance because of how you treated them, your wish to reconnect doesn’t override their choice. If they have asked for no contact or blocked you, don’t go around it through friends, relatives or new accounts. That’s pressure, and it can become harassment.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What Earl knows. What he said, and that it was unfair. That Opal had surgery. That he misses her.

What he doesn’t know. How Opal remembers the fight. Whether she wants contact. How she’s recovering. He won’t ask the cousin to find out for him.

Who decides. Earl decides whether to reach out, once, and how. Opal decides whether to answer and how much contact she wants. Nobody else should act as a go-between unless Opal chooses that.

If it’s an ex. Ask yourself honestly what you want. If the answer is “to change their mind,” wait. That isn’t contact on equal terms. Reasons that can work include an apology you owe, a practical matter, or replying when they’ve reached out first. Chapter 25, Dating, Intimacy, and Difficult Relationships, shows how to judge it when an ex contacts you. There’s a short example with an ex near the end of this playbook.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Earl

  • Why now: her surgery reminded me that time is short for both of us.
  • What I hope for: to be back in touch. The smallest version I’d be glad of: one phone call.
  • What I’m responsible for: saying she abandoned Mom.
  • What I won’t ask for: an apology in return, an explanation, or a quick visit.
  • The Clean Ask, as a card: “Opal, I heard you had surgery, and I hope you’re recovering well. I’ve thought about you a lot. I’m sorry for what I said after Mom’s funeral. It wasn’t true, and I was wrong to say it. I’d like to be back in touch, at whatever pace suits you, if you want that. There’s no pressure to reply. Earl” (plus his phone number).
  • The No-Agreement Plan: If she doesn’t reply, I take that as her answer for now. I won’t write again unless she contacts me. I’ll talk it over with my friend Basil from church, and get on with my life.
  • Fairness check: no guilt (“we’re not getting younger”), no relatives sent to persuade her, no surprise visit.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
Opal calls three weeks after the card arrives.

Opal: “I got your card. I didn’t expect it.”

Earl: “Thanks for calling. How are you feeling?”

Opal: “Better. Slow. What do you want, Earl?”

Earl: “Nothing complicated. I’m sorry for what I said. And I don’t want us to be strangers.”

Opal: “You said I abandoned Mom. In front of everyone.”

Earl: “I did. It wasn’t true, and it was cruel. I’m sorry.”

Opal: “I drove up every other weekend for two years.”

Earl: “I know you did.”

Earl doesn’t add his side of the story. Today isn’t for that.

Opal: “I’m not ready to act like nothing happened.”

Earl: “You don’t have to. I’d just like to talk now and then, if you want that.”

Opal: “Maybe. Call me after Christmas. Not before.”

Earl: “After Christmas. I’ll call the first week of January.”

Opal: “Okay. Bye, Earl.”

Nine minutes, and one call promised. After nine years of silence, that’s a real opening.

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Go slowly. Small, steady contact rebuilds more trust than one big emotional talk. Let the history come up when both of you are ready, and listen before you explain.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Opal agreed to one call, with conditions. Others may want news by email but no visits, or want to talk about the past before anything else. Follow their pace. “Maybe” is an answer to respect, not a door to push.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: “I don’t want contact.” Or no reply at all. Respect it. If they replied, you can say once: “I understand. I won’t keep reaching out. If that ever changes, I’m here. Take care.” Then stop. Don’t recruit relatives or send a second, longer letter. Leaving them alone is the most respectful thing you can do.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html: They cancel the call, go quiet again, or the old argument flares on the second call. Don’t chase. Say once, “That’s okay. I’m here if you want to talk.” If old patterns of harm return, from either side, you’re allowed to step back too.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
“Good to hear your voice, Opal. I’ll call the first week of January, like we said. Take care of yourself.”

Then call when you said you would.

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Sometimes the door stays shut. That’s a loss, and it’s normal to grieve it. You still did your part: a real apology, asked once, with the answer respected. Chapter 28, When They Still Say No, covers living with a closed door. Chapter 29, Your Next Chapter Starts Here, covers building support elsewhere: one person, one place, one regular thing.

parts.heading: A short example with an ex
parts.html:
Wade is forty-eight. Three years ago he ended a two-year relationship with Paloma by text, the night before a trip they had planned. They haven’t spoken since. She never asked him not to contact her, and she hasn’t blocked him. He still has her late father’s toolbox in his garage.

Wade checks his reasons first. He isn’t hoping to get back together. He owes her an apology, and he has something of hers to return. Both are his to settle, and neither needs her to feel anything in return.

He sends one short email:

“Paloma, I still have your dad’s toolbox, and I’d like to get it back to you. I can ship it wherever you choose. I also owe you an apology. Ending things by text, the night before our trip, was unkind, and I’m sorry. I’m not asking for anything else. Wade”

Four days later she replies: “Ship it to my office, address below. I don’t want to talk, and please don’t write again.”

That’s a clear no, and Wade treats it as one. He ships the toolbox to her office that week, with no note inside and no email to say it’s on its way. The parcel itself is the only reply. Then he stops. No birthday message, no asking mutual friends how she’s doing, no “just checking it arrived.”

He got the toolbox back to her and said what he owed. He didn’t get a conversation, and his plan never depended on one. If she ever contacts him, he can answer. Until then, her no stands.

parts.html:

  • What I hope for (smallest version): one phone call.
  • What I’m responsible for: saying she abandoned Mom.
  • What I won’t ask for: an apology back, a quick visit.
  • How I’ll reach out: a card, with my number.
  • What I’ll do if there’s no reply: take it as her answer; no second letter.
  • Who I’ll talk to either way: Basil.

playbooks.title: Stepping back from a group or a role you've outgrown

parts.heading: The situation
parts.html:
Zora is fifty-eight. For nine years she has coordinated the Saturday volunteer crew at a community food pantry. She schedules about twenty-five volunteers, trains new ones, and opens the building at 7 a.m. every Saturday.

She still believes in the pantry. But her knees are worse, her grandchildren are at the age where Saturdays matter, and she has started dreading Friday nights. She wants to step down and stay on as a volunteer one Saturday a month. The director, Wes, relies on her, and she expects guilt, some of it from herself.

The same playbook works for other roles you’ve outgrown: club treasurer, the friend who organizes every trip, the relative who always hosts.

parts.heading: What you know, what you don't, and who decides
parts.html:
What Zora knows. Everything the role involves, and that two volunteers, Ruth and Manny, have helped with scheduling before.

What she doesn’t know. Whether anyone wants the job. Whether it should be split between two people. How Wes will react.

Who decides. Zora decides whether she continues and what help she offers on the way out. Wes decides how the role gets filled. In a volunteer role, Zora doesn’t need permission to step down. In a paid job, check your contract for notice rules. Playbook 5, Leaving a job well, covers that.

parts.heading: Your preparation sheet
parts.html:
Completed example: Zora

  • My decision: I’m stepping down as coordinator at the end of March.
  • The Clean Ask, about the handover, not the decision: “I’d like us to plan the handover together. I’ll write down how the role works and train whoever takes it on through March. I’d like to stay on as a volunteer one Saturday a month. Who do you think we should ask?”
  • Likely pushback: “Nobody else knows how.” “The families depend on Saturdays.” “Can you stay until summer?” “Just be on call.”
  • The one thing I won’t do: agree to stay “until someone’s found,” with no end date.
  • The No-Agreement Plan: I step down on March 31 either way. Before then, I’ll finish the written guide and give Wes the volunteer list, following the pantry’s rules on contact details. I’ll stay one extra month only if a named person is training with me.
  • Fairness check: real notice and real help, without staying out of guilt.

parts.heading: The conversation
parts.html:
After closing on a Saturday, in Wes’s office.

Zora: “Wes, I’ve made a decision. I’m stepping down as Saturday coordinator at the end of March. I’d like to stay on as a volunteer one Saturday a month.”

Wes: “Zora, no. Nobody else knows how Saturdays work.”

Zora: “That’s why I’m telling you now, with two months to go. I’ll write down how it all works, and I’ll train whoever takes it on.”

Wes: “The families depend on us. If Saturdays fall apart…”

Zora: “I care about that too. That’s why I want a proper handover, not a sudden exit.”

Wes: “Could you stay until summer? Things are crazy right now.”

Zora: “No. March 31 is my last day as coordinator. If someone is training with me by then, I could stay through April to help them.”

Wes: “Could you at least be on call? In case something goes wrong?”

Zora: “I won’t be on call. I’ll answer questions by email for the first month.”

Wes: “This is going to be hard.”

Zora: “I know. Ruth and Manny have both done scheduling. Could we ask them about sharing it?”

Wes: “I’ll ask Ruth. Manny’s busy. I still wish you’d reconsider.”

Zora: “I understand. I’ve decided. Can we meet next Saturday to go through the guide?”

Wes: “Fine. Next Saturday.”

parts.heading: If they agree
parts.html: Make the handover real: training dates, the finished guide, and introducing the new person yourself. After your end date, let them do it their way, even if they change things you built.

parts.heading: If they partly agree
parts.html: Wes accepted the date but asked for “on call.” Offer what you’re willing to do, with limits, then stop. Help with an end date is generous. Help with no end date is the old role under another name.

parts.heading: If they refuse
parts.html: “We can’t let you go.” In a volunteer role, they can’t stop you. Stay warm and repeat the date. If the group chat fills with “You’re irreplaceable,” thank people and don’t reopen the decision. Chapter 27, Groups, Media, and Manufactured Pressure, covers what to do when a group leans on you.

parts.heading: If they agree and then backtrack
parts.html: In late March: “Still nobody. Can you just do April?” Go back to what you said: “I said I’d stay through April if someone was training with me. Is anyone?” If not, step down on the date. If Saturday calls keep coming afterward, answer by email during the week, as agreed.

parts.heading: The follow-up message
parts.html:
An email to Wes the same day:

“Thanks for hearing me out today. To confirm: my last day as Saturday coordinator is March 31. I’ll have the written guide to you by February 15 and can train someone on February 22 and March 1. After March, I’ll answer questions by email through April, and I’d like to volunteer on the first Saturday of each month.”

parts.heading: If agreement never comes
parts.html: Sometimes nobody steps up. That still isn’t a reason to stay forever. Leave the guide, tell the volunteers who to contact, and step down on your date. If the group cools toward you, Chapter 28, When They Still Say No, covers being left out after a no. And as Chapter 29, Your Next Chapter Starts Here, points out, the time that opens up fills quickly. Decide what you want in it before someone else does.

outro.heading: Where to go from here
outro.html:
These playbooks take the book’s tools into twenty specific situations. When a situation doesn’t fit any of them, go back to the tools themselves. The Power Map is in Chapter 2, Read the Power Map. The Clean Ask is in Chapter 17, Ask for More and Negotiate Well. The Smallest Agreed Step is in Chapter 22, Turn Agreement Into Action. The No-Agreement Plan is in Chapter 28, When They Still Say No. The Four Fair Influence Tests are in Chapter 30, Power Without Becoming What You Resent.

If pressure ever turns into fear, threats, or control of your money, phone or movements, stop using these playbooks and go to Chapter 11, When Pressure Becomes Danger. If you want steady practice between big conversations, Part VII, The 21-Day Power Reset, starts with Chapter 31, Your Three-Day Quick Start.
